The second trap is using 발전하다 transitively; to actively develop something you need the causative 발전시키다 (기술을 발전시켰어요), never 기술을 발전했어요.
발전하다.explanation: "to develop, to advance, to progress" in Korean is 발전하다 (baljeonhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 발전해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 발전하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 기술이 빠르게 발전하고 있어요. ("Technology is developing fast.") — then reshape the same stem into 발전하고 싶어요 (desire), 발전할 수 있어요 (ability), and 발전할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
발전하다.shortExplanation: 발전하다 means "to develop, to advance, to progress" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 발전하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 발전해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't mix up 발전하다 (develop/advance) with 발견하다 (discover) — one syllable apart, completely different meanings.
To say 'develop X' transitively, use the causative 발전시키다: 기술을 발전시켰어요, not 기술을 발전했어요.
Mark the 'into' goal with ~(으)로, not 을/를: 사업으로 발전했어요 (developed into a business), not 사업을 발전했어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 발전하다 becomes 발전할 수 있어요 ("can") and 발전할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I develop, to advance, to progress.
I do not develop, to advance, to progress.
I want to develop, to advance, to progress.
I can develop, to advance, to progress.
I have to develop, to advance, to progress.

usagePhrases.note: The thing that develops takes 이/가 — 발전하다 is intransitive (기술이/경제가 발전하다).

examples.en: Our neighborhood has developed a lot.
examples.note: Casual 발전했어 — for places and economies visibly growing over time.

examples.en: If you keep at it, your skills will improve.
examples.note: 실력이 발전하다 = one's skills advance — an encouraging line about steady progress.

examples.en: A small spat escalated into a big fight.
examples.note: Real-situation — 발전하다 can mean a situation escalates ~(으)로 into something bigger, often negative.

ex.en: I think traditions still exist.
ex.note: 생각해요 (I think) also uses the 다고 pattern: 존재한다고 생각해요. 생각하다 is another common reporting verb alongside 하다.

존재하다.nuance: 존재하다 (存在, 'remain + be present') means 'to exist' in an abstract, weighty, or emphatic sense — common in writing, debate, philosophy, and serious topics. Its everyday near-synonym is 있다, and the line is sharp: for 'there is / I have' you must use 있다 (책이 있어요, 질문이 있어요), never 존재하다. Reach for 존재하다 only when you want to spotlight the very fact of something's existence — a method, a being, a problem — or to deny it categorically with 존재하지 않아요. It is intransitive, so the thing that exists takes 이/가 and there is no object. The big English-speaker pitfall is mapping every English 'exist/there is' onto 존재하다: 'there's a café nearby' is 근처에 카페가 있어요, and saying 카페가 존재해요 sounds comically grand. Keep 존재하다 for the abstract and the philosophical.
존재하다.explanation: 존재하다 (jonjaehada) means "to exist". Start from the polite form 존재해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 존재하다. A strong first sentence is 그런 방법은 존재하지 않아요. ("Such a method doesn't exist."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 존재하다 also becomes 존재하고 싶어요 (want), 존재할 수 있어요 (can), and 존재할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
존재하다.shortExplanation: 존재하다 means "to exist" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 존재하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 존재해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't replace everyday 있다 with 존재하다 — 'I have a question' is 질문이 있어요, not 질문이 존재해요; 'there's a store' is 가게가 있어요.
The natural negative is 존재하지 않아요; clipping it to 존재 안 해요 sounds off-register for such an abstract verb.
Treating it as transitive — there is no 존재하다 with 을/를; the existing thing always takes 이/가 (생명체가 존재하다).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 존재하다 becomes 존재할 수 있어요 ("can") and 존재할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: 존재하지 않아요 is the natural way to deny existence flatly — 'there's no such thing.'

examples.en: Does Santa Claus really exist?
examples.note: Casual 존재해? to a child or friend — the contracted 하 + 어 → 해 form.

examples.en: That problem has existed for a long time.
examples.note: 오래전부터 존재했어요 stresses a problem has 'been there' all along, not just appeared.

examples.en: Prejudice still exists in our society.
examples.note: Formal 존재합니다 with 여전히 (still) fits essays and serious discussion about society.

참여하다.en: to participate / to take part in

ex.en: The teacher said to be sure to participate in the event.
ex.note: This is a reported command (not statement) → -(으)라고: 참여하라고 하셨어요. Compare with 다고 (statement) and 냐고 (question).

참여하다.nuance: 참여하다 (參與, '參 take part + 與 join in') means to actively take part in and contribute to an activity, event, or process, so its core is involvement, not physical presence. The single most useful contrast for a learner: 참석하다 (出席) is simply attending — being bodily present at a meeting, wedding, or ceremony — whereas 참여하다 means you actually engage and add something. You 참석 a friend's wedding (you show up and sit there), but you 참여 a project or campaign (you roll up your sleeves); a related word 가담하다 is 'join in' with a negative slant (joining a crime or a fight). What you join is marked with 에 (행사에 참여하다), and it pairs habitually with 적극적으로 and the bare noun in 참여율 (participation rate), 시민 참여 (citizen participation), 참여형 (participatory). As a regular 하다-verb it is 참여해요 / 참여했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is using one word for both 'attend' and 'participate' the way English does — if you only mean you were physically there, say 참석했어요; save 참여했어요 for when you genuinely took part.
참여하다.explanation: 참여하다 (chamyeohada) = "to participate / to take part in". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 참여해요 plus one useful sentence like 행사에 참여하다 ("to take part in an event"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 참여하고 싶어요 for what you want, 참여할 수 있어요 for what you can, 참여 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
참여하다.shortExplanation: 참여하다 means "to participate / to take part in" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 참여하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 참여해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 참여하다 when you only attended without contributing: for 'I attended the ceremony' say 행사에 참석했어요; 참여하다 implies you actively engaged, which can overstate a passive presence.
Marking the activity with 을/를 (행사를 참여해요). What you join takes 에: 행사에 참여해요 — you take part *in* it, so the locative-style particle is required.
Treating 참여하다 and 참석하다 as freely interchangeable. They differ in meaning: 참석 = be present, 참여 = get involved, and picking the wrong one misstates how engaged you were.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 참여하다 becomes 참여할 수 있어요 ("can") and 참여할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I participate / to take part in.
I do not participate / to take part in.
I want to participate / to take part in.
I can participate / to take part in.
I have to participate / to take part in.
to take part in an event
usagePhrases.note: 참여하다 takes 에 for the activity you join: 토론에 참여해요 = I take part in the discussion.

examples.en: I want to take part in that gathering too.
examples.note: Basic 에 marking plus 고 싶다; 참여하다 already implies you'll actually join in, not just watch.

examples.en: I actively took part in this volunteer activity.
examples.note: 적극적으로 collocates strongly; 참여하다 stresses hands-on involvement rather than mere attendance.

examples.ko: 회의에 참여는 했지만 의견은 한마디도 안 냈어요.
examples.romanization: hoeuie chamyeoneun haetjiman uigyeoneun hanmadido an naesseoyo.
examples.en: I took part in the meeting but didn't say a single word.
examples.note: Splitting 참여 + 는 + 했다 adds contrast, showing 참여하다 is active involvement you can still hold back within.

ex.en: Even as society changes rapidly, traditions remain.
ex.note: 변해도 = even though (it) changes (-(아/어)도 concessive). 남다 (to remain) contrasts with 변하다 (to change) in this classic Chapter 36 sentence.

변하다.nuance: 변하다 is Sino-Korean: 變 (byeon, 'change, transform') + 하다, so it carries the feeling of something turning into a different state on its own, by nature or over time. The sharp contrast English speakers must learn is 변하다 vs 바꾸다: 변하다 is intransitive — the thing changes by itself (날씨가 변해요 = the weather changes), while 바꾸다 is transitive — somebody deliberately swaps or replaces a thing (계획을 바꿔요 = I change the plan). A related pair is 변하다 vs 바뀌다 (the passive of 바꾸다): 바뀌다 implies an external switch (신호등이 바뀌었어요 = the traffic light switched), whereas 변하다 implies inner transformation (성격이 변했어요 = his personality changed). Register is neutral and everyday. The big pitfall is using 변하다 with a direct object — you cannot say *계획을 변해요 to mean 'I change the plan'; if there is an actor doing the changing, you need 바꾸다. 변하다 only ever describes the subject itself becoming different.
변하다.explanation: 변하다 (byeonhada) means "to change". Start from the polite form 변해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 변하다. A strong first sentence is 많이 변했어요 ("You've changed a lot"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 변하다 also becomes 변하고 싶어요 (want), 변할 수 있어요 (can), and 변할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
변하다.shortExplanation: 변하다 means "to change" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 변하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 변해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 머리 스타일을 변했어요 for 'I changed my hairstyle' — 변하다 takes no object. Because you actively did it, use 바꿨어요 (from 바꾸다): 머리 스타일을 바꿨어요.

Confusing 변하다 with 바뀌다. If something was switched/replaced by an outside force (a schedule, a signal), Koreans say 바뀌었어요; reserve 변했어요 for internal transformation like feelings, color, or personality.
Over-using 변하다 for small everyday swaps. 'I changed my clothes' is 옷을 갈아입었어요, not 옷이 변했어요 — 변하다 would weirdly mean the clothes themselves morphed.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 변하다 becomes 변할 수 있어요 ("can") and 변할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Said to friends not seen in years

examples.en: The color of the sky changed
examples.note: Simple visible change, past tense

examples.ko: 요즘 그 친구가 좀 변한 것 같아요
examples.romanization: yojeum geu chinguga jom byeonhan geot gatayo
examples.en: That friend seems to have changed a bit lately
examples.note: -ㄴ 것 같아요 softens it to an impression

examples.ko: 사람 마음은 언제든지 변할 수 있어요
examples.romanization: saram maeumeun eonjedeunji byeonhal su isseoyo
examples.en: A person's heart can change at any time
examples.note: 변할 수 있어요 expresses possibility

ex.en: I decided to start a small business.
ex.note: 기로 했어요 — a settled decision to begin the business

사업.nuance: 사업 (事業, literally 'affair-work') is business as an active undertaking — running a company, launching a commercial project, or being self-employed. The key boundary is against 산업 (産業, industry as a whole sector): 사업 is what one person or firm concretely does, while 산업 is the field that many businesses belong to (자동차 산업 = the auto industry, but 자동차 사업 = a particular auto-related business venture). It is also broader than the English word — a government or non-profit project is a 사업 too (복지 사업 = welfare project), so don't restrict it to 'for-profit'. Register is neutral; everyone from a small shop owner to a CEO uses it. The classic English-speaker pitfall is treating 사업하다 as a fixed block: the moment an object marker appears you must break it apart (사업을 하다, 사업을 시작하다), never 사업하다를. Also resist translating 'do business with someone' word-for-word — Koreans say 거래하다 (to trade/deal) for that, not 사업을 하다.
사업.explanation: "business; enterprise; venture" is 사업 (saeop). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 사업을 하다 ("to run a business"). Watch the particle attached to 사업 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.
사업.shortExplanation: 사업 means "business; enterprise; venture" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 사업 (a venture you actively run) with 산업 (an industry sector): say 자동차 산업이 발전했다 for the sector, but 그는 자동차 사업을 한다 for one person's business.
사업하다 is one verb, but adding the object marker forces a split: 사업을 하다, never 사업하다를.
'Do business with a partner' is not 그 사람과 사업을 하다 — Koreans say 그 사람과 거래하다 (to deal/trade with) for an ongoing commercial relationship.

usagePhrases.note: 사업하다 is also one verb; once you add the object marker 을 you must split it: 사업을 하다
시작하다 = to begin; 사업을 차리다 (to set up a business) is a more colloquial alternative
잘되다 is one word and intransitive; the opposite is 사업이 안되다 (business is doing badly)
계획 = plan; 사업 모델, 사업 분야, 사업 자금 also use 사업 as a bare modifier (no 의)

examples.en: I want to run a small business.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 사업을 하다 split by 을; 작은 modifies 사업

examples.ko: 요즘 경기가 안 좋아서 사업이 잘 안돼요.
examples.romanization: yojeum gyeonggiga an joaseo saeobi jal andwaeyo.
examples.en: Business isn't going well these days because the economy is bad.
examples.note: 안돼요 = isn't going well; -아서 gives the reason and can't take a past tense before it

examples.ko: 그분은 맨손으로 시작해서 사업으로 크게 성공한 분이에요.
examples.romanization: geubuneun maensoneuro sijakaeseo saeobeuro keuge seonggonghan bunieyo.
examples.en: He started from nothing and made it big in business.
examples.note: 사업으로 = through/in business; 맨손으로 = with bare hands, a real-life success-story phrase

ex.en: I ended up starting a new project.
ex.note: 게 됐어요 — the project arose through circumstances, not purely personal choice

시작하다.nuance: 시작하다 means 'to start / begin' and is a Sino-Korean 하다 verb — 시작 (始作, literally 始 'begin' + 作 'make/do', i.e. 'set in motion') plus 하다. As a 하다 verb it conjugates regularly with 하다 → 해요: 시작해요 / 시작합니다 / 시작했어요. A point that trips learners is that 시작하다 works both transitively and intransitively: with a doer it takes an object (저는 일을 시작해요 'I start work', 을/를), and with no doer the thing simply begins and takes the subject marker (수업이 시작해요 'class starts', 이/가). Contrast it with the pure intransitive 시작되다 (始作되다, 'to be started/begin'), which is more formal and never takes an object — 회의가 시작됐어요 'the meeting began'. Its natural opposite is 끝나다 ('to end'). The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) conjugating the 하다 wrongly as 시작하요 instead of 시작해요, and (2) forcing an object onto the no-doer case (수업을 시작해요 when you simply mean class begins) — when nothing actively starts it, use 수업이 시작해요 or the passive 시작돼요.
시작하다.explanation: 시작하다 (sijakhada) = "to start". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 시작해요 plus one useful sentence like 일을 시작해요 ("I start work"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 시작하고 싶어요 for what you want, 시작할 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 시작해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations.
시작하다.shortExplanation: 시작하다 means "to start" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 시작하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 시작해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Conjugating the 하다 as 시작하요 — every 하다 verb becomes 해요, so it is 시작해요 (formal 시작합니다, past 시작했어요).
Forcing an object when there is no doer (수업을 시작해요 to mean 'class begins') — use the intransitive 수업이 시작해요, or 시작돼요.
Using the formal passive 시작되다 in casual speech where active 시작하다 fits — keep 시작되다 for announcements/writing (회의가 시작됩니다).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 시작하다 becomes 시작할 수 있어요 ("can") and 시작할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: with an object (transitive) the thing started takes 을/를

examples.en: Class starts at nine.
examples.note: time at 에; intransitive, so 수업이

examples.en: I started a new job last month.
examples.note: transitive past; 일을 시작했어요

examples.en: Ready? Then shall we start now?
examples.note: real suggestion before an activity

cluster.title: 시작하다 vs 출발하다
cluster.rule: English "start" covers both, but Korean never mixes them: 시작하다 is an activity beginning (class, work, a movie), 출발하다 is a person or vehicle physically leaving the starting point. You can 출발하다 for school and 시작하다 the class after you arrive.

members.hint: physically setting off from a place

ex.en: I can't even sleep because I'm afraid of failing.
ex.note: 실패하다 → 실패할까 봐: feared outcome expressed with -(으)ㄹ까 봐

실패하다.nuance: 실패하다 means that an attempt, plan, project, or goal did not achieve its intended result. The target commonly takes 에: 사업에 실패하다, 시도에 실패하다. For exams and auditions, Korean often chooses the more specific 떨어지다 or 불합격하다 instead of the heavier 시험에 실패하다. Keep 실패하다 separate from 실수하다: 실패 is an unsuccessful overall result, while 실수 is a mistake made during the process. A failed attempt can be retried; a mistake can happen even inside a successful project.
실패하다.explanation: 실패하다 (silpaehada) means "to fail." Use N에 실패하다 for the attempt or goal that did not work, and use 실패할까 봐 when fear of failure causes another action. Do not use it for every small error; that is usually 실수하다.
실패하다.shortExplanation: 실패하다 describes an unsuccessful result; 실수하다 describes a mistake during the process.
commonMistakes: Saying 시험을 실패했어요. Use 시험에 실패했어요, or more naturally for a test, 시험에 떨어졌어요.
Confusing 실패하다 with 실수하다. A typo is a 실수; an entire plan that did not work is a 실패.
Using 실패하다 whenever English says ‘fail to do.’ Often 못 + verb is more natural: 연락하지 못했어요, not 연락하는 데 실패했어요 in ordinary speech.
Writing 실패 하다 with a space. The verb is one word: 실패하다.

conjugationTips.title: 하다 verb
conjugationTips.body: 실패하다 conjugates regularly: 실패해요, 실패했어요, 실패할 거예요. Before -(으)ㄹ까 봐, it becomes 실패할까 봐.

usagePhrases.note: The failed field or attempt takes 에.
A neutral way to report an unsuccessful attempt.

usagePhrases.en: I am worried that I might fail.

usagePhrases.note: Here 실패 is a noun and takes 를.

examples.ko: 첫 번째 시도는 실패했지만 두 번째에는 성공했어요.
examples.romanization: cheot beonjjae sidoneun silpaehaetjiman du beonjjaeeneun seonggonghaesseoyo.
examples.en: The first attempt failed, but the second one succeeded.
examples.note: Contrasts the result words 실패하다 and 성공하다.

examples.ko: 실패할까 봐 시작도 안 하면 아무것도 배울 수 없어요.
examples.romanization: silpaehalkka bwa sijakdo an hamyeon amugeotdo baeul su eopseoyo.
examples.en: If you do not even start because you are afraid of failing, you cannot learn anything.
examples.note: Fear of failure is the cause of not starting.

examples.ko: 발표에서 단어 하나를 잘못 말한 건 실수지만, 준비한 내용을 전혀 전달하지 못한 건 실패에 가까워요.
examples.romanization: balpyoeseo daneo hanareul jalmot malhan geon silsujiman, junbihan naeyongeul jeonhyeo jeondalhaji mothan geon silpaee gakkawoyo.
examples.en: Saying one word incorrectly in a presentation is a mistake, but failing to communicate any of the prepared content is closer to an overall failure.
examples.note: Clarifies the scale difference between one mistake and an unsuccessful overall result.

ex.en: As I kept working hard, I came to succeed.
ex.note: 하다 보니까 + 게 됐어요: a natural combination — persistent effort led to the circumstantial outcome

성공하다.nuance: 성공하다 means reaching a desired result in a project, career, business, experiment, or attempt. The field or task commonly takes 에: 사업에 성공하다, 다이어트에 성공하다, 예약에 성공하다. Korean often uses more specific verbs where English broadly says ‘succeed’: pass an exam is 시험에 합격하다, win a competition is 대회에서 우승하다, and a plan ‘goes well’ is 일이 잘되다. 성공하다 can sound goal-focused and substantial, while 잘되다 is the more conversational choice for something simply turning out well.
성공하다.explanation: 성공하다 (seonggonghada) means "to succeed." Use N에 성공하다 for the goal or task achieved. When the situation only ‘went well,’ 잘됐어요 may sound more natural than calling it a major success.
성공하다.shortExplanation: 성공하다 means achieving a goal, usually in the pattern N에 성공하다.
commonMistakes: Using 을/를 for the achieved task: 사업을 성공했어요. Say 사업에 성공했어요.
Saying 시험에 성공했어요 for passing an exam. The normal phrase is 시험에 합격했어요.
Confusing 성공하다 with 성공시키다. 성공하다 is intransitive; 성공시키다 means to make a project or person succeed.
Using 성공했어요 for every small thing that went smoothly. In casual speech, 잘됐어요 often fits better.

conjugationTips.title: 하다 verb
conjugationTips.body: 성공하다 is regular: 성공해요, 성공했어요, 성공할 거예요. The result phrase 성공하게 되다 means circumstances led to success.

usagePhrases.note: The field of success takes 에.
A more formal collocation used in reports and news.

examples.ko: 여러 번 연습한 끝에 발표를 성공적으로 마쳤어요.
examples.romanization: yeoreo beon yeonseupan kkeute balpyoreul seonggongjeogeuro machyeosseoyo.
examples.en: After practicing many times, I finished the presentation successfully.
examples.note: 성공적으로 is the adverb ‘successfully.’

examples.ko: 예약에 성공하려면 오픈 시간에 바로 접속해야 해요.
examples.romanization: yeyage seonggongharyeomyeon opeun sigane baro jeopsokhaeya haeyo.
examples.en: To succeed in making the reservation, you need to log in right when booking opens.
examples.note: A realistic high-demand reservation context.

examples.romanization: siheomeneun hapgyeokhaetgo, junbihan peurojekteudo jal dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: I passed the exam, and the project I prepared also went well.
examples.note: Uses more natural specific verbs instead of repeating 성공하다.

ex.ko: 걱정이 많아서 잠을 잘 못 자요.
ex.en: I have so many worries that I can't sleep well.
ex.note: 걱정이 많다 — literally 'worries are many'; Korean treats worry as a countable thing

걱정.nuance: 걱정 is care or anxiety about something uncertain — the knot in your stomach over a result, a person's health, or money. It splits across two verbs: active 걱정하다 ('to worry about X,' X = object → 건강을 걱정해요) and spontaneous 걱정이 되다 ('X worries me / I become worried,' the worry arises → subject 이). Contrast 걱정 with 고민 (a problem you are mulling over, more like deliberation/a dilemma you turn in your mind) and with 불안 不安 (free-floating anxiety/unease without a clear object): you 걱정 about a specific thing, you 고민 over a decision, you feel 불안 as a mood. The most useful chunk is 걱정하지 마세요/걱정 마 — the go-to way to comfort someone. The English-speaker pitfall is the 하다 particle error 걱정이 해요 (use 걱정을 해요), and saying 걱정에 대해 생각해요 when you simply mean 걱정해요.
걱정.explanation: "worry" is 걱정 (geokjeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 걱정을 해요 ("I worry"). Watch the particle attached to 걱정 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
걱정.shortExplanation: 걱정 means "worry" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 걱정이 해요. With 하다 the worry is the object → 걱정을 해요 (or just 걱정해요).
Using 걱정해 for mulling over a choice. Deliberating a decision is 고민하다 (진로를 고민해요), while 걱정 is anxious care.
Forgetting the object marker: '엄마가 제 건강 걱정해요' is casual-OK, but the full form is 건강을 걱정해요 — the thing worried about takes 을.

usagePhrases.en: I have a lot of worries

usagePhrases.note: 걱정이 되다 = worry arises on its own

examples.en: These days I have a lot of worries.
examples.note: Simple: 걱정이 많다 — worries exist (subject 이).

examples.en: My mom worries about my health.
examples.note: Everyday: 걱정하다 takes what's worried about as object (건강을).

examples.en: Don't worry. Everything will be fine.
examples.note: Real situation: 걱정하지 마세요 + reassurance, very natural comfort.

ex.en: I've already decided. I've made up my mind.
ex.note: 결정했어요 and 기로 했어요 both express decisions, but 기로 했어요 attaches to the specific action decided upon

결정하다.nuance: 결정하다 is built on the 한자 決定 (決 'resolve, cut through' + 定 'fix, settle'), so it literally means 'cut through and settle' — reaching a firm choice after deliberation. Three near-synonyms divide the space: 정하다 is the everyday, lighter 'set/decide' (그냥 정해요 = let's just settle it); 선택하다 (選擇) is 'select' from given options; 고르다 is the casual 'pick' (고르다 a fruit, a color). Use 결정하다 for consequential, considered decisions (a job, a move, a date) — for which thing to pick off a shelf, 고르다 or 선택하다 fits better. To decide to DO an action, the partner pattern is -기로 결정하다 (가기로 결정했어요); English speakers often forget the -기로 and say 결정했어요 가다. As a 하다 verb the negative splits: 결정 안 해요, 결정 못 해요. The heavier idiom 결정을 내리다 frames it as 'handing down' a decision.
결정하다.explanation: "to decide" in Korean is 결정하다 (gyeoljeonghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 결정해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 결정하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 메뉴를 결정했어요. ("I decided on the menu.") — then reshape the same stem into 결정하고 싶어요 (desire), 결정할 수 있어요 (ability), and 결정 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
결정하다.shortExplanation: 결정하다 means "to decide" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 결정하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 결정해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 고르다 (pick) for a major life decision: '회사를 그만두는 것을 골랐어요' sounds like choosing off a menu. Say 그만두기로 결정했어요.
Forgetting -기로 when deciding to do something: '결정했어요 한국에 가다' is ungrammatical. Embed it: 한국에 가기로 결정했어요.
Forming the negative as 안 결정해요. Inside the 하다 verb: 결정 안 해요 (or 아직 결정 못 했어요 for 'haven't decided yet').

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 결정하다 becomes 결정할 수 있어요 ("can") and 결정할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Thing chosen takes 을/를; 결정하다 = settle the matter.

examples.en: Did you decide what to eat?
examples.note: Casual; -ㄹ지 (what/whether) embeds the open question before 결정하다.

examples.ko: 여행 날짜를 아직 결정 못 했어요.
examples.romanization: yeohaeng naljjareul ajik gyeoljeong mo taesseoyo.
examples.en: I still can't decide the travel date.
examples.note: 결정 못 하다 = unable to settle on it; 못 sits inside the 하다 verb.

examples.en: I decided to quit the company.
examples.note: Big life choice with -기로 결정하다; this is where 결정하다 outshines 정하다.

ex.en: I decided to give it a try.
ex.note: 도전해 보기로 했어요 — 해 보다 (try doing) + 기로 했어요: decided to at least attempt

도전하다.nuance: 도전하다 = to take something on, rise to a challenge, brave a new or daunting endeavor — overwhelmingly positive and aspirational (a job change, a new hobby, scary spicy food, a hard exam). The hanja 挑戰 literally means 挑 'provoke, stir up' + 戰 'battle', i.e. 'to pick a fight', and that combative root explains both senses: figuratively you 'do battle' with a goal. Particle pitfall for English speakers: it takes 에, not 을/를 — 마라톤에 도전하다 ('take on the marathon'), 시험에 도전하다. Contrast it with 노력하다 (sustained, grinding effort over time) and 시도하다 (a neutral, often one-off 'attempt'): 도전하다 specifically frames the target as bold or intimidating, with a brave-the-unknown flavor. Note: it does NOT mean confronting a person in an argument — 'to challenge someone' in that sense is 이의를 제기하다 or 도전장을 내밀다, not plain 도전하다. The everyday encouragement is 도전해 봐.
도전하다.explanation: 도전하다 (dojeonhada) means "to take on a challenge". Start from the polite form 도전해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 도전하다. A strong first sentence is 한번 도전해 봐 ("Give it a shot"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 도전하다 also becomes 도전하고 싶어 (want), 도전할 수 있어 (can), and 도전 못 해 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
도전하다.shortExplanation: 도전하다 means "to take on a challenge" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 도전하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 도전해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 을/를 instead of 에 — it's 마라톤에 도전하다 ('take on the marathon'), not 마라톤을 도전하다.
Using 도전하다 to mean 'challenge a claim/person' — to dispute something, say 이의를 제기하다; 도전하다 is for taking on a goal or feat, not arguing back.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 도전하다 becomes 도전할 수 있어 ("can") and 도전할 거야 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not take on a challenge.
I want to take on a challenge.
I can take on a challenge.
I have to take on a challenge.

usagePhrases.note: Encouraging someone to try something new/bold; 한번 = 'just once, give it a go'.

examples.en: This year I'm going to try taking on a marathon.
examples.note: ~에 도전하다; ~(으)려고 = 'I intend/plan to'. Common New Year goal talk.

examples.en: I changed jobs because I wanted to take on a new field.
examples.note: 이직하다 = 'to change jobs', big in 20-30s career talk; 분야 = field/area.

examples.ko: 매운 거 잘 못 먹는데 불닭볶음면 한번 도전해 볼게.
examples.romanization: maeun geo jal mon meongneunde buldalkbokkeummyeon hanbeon dojeonhae bolge.
examples.en: I'm bad with spicy food but I'll give fire-noodles a try.
examples.note: 불닭볶음면 = the famous super-spicy instant noodle; 도전해 볼게 = 'I'll give it a try'.

ex.en: I'm worried that my income might decrease.
ex.note: 줄어들다 → 줄어들까 봐: the feared outcome is shrinking income

수입.nuance: 수입 for personal money means income or revenue — the money coming in — and lives in opposition to 지출 (spending going out). Crucially it is a homograph hiding two different hanja: 收入 ('gather + enter') is income, while 輸入 ('transport + enter') is imports, the opposite of 수출 (輸出, exports). Spoken aloud they are identical, so only context tells you whether 수입 means a paycheck or a shipment of foreign goods; in an economics lecture both senses can appear in one paragraph. The near-synonym for the income sense is 소득 (所得, already in vocab): 소득 is the more formal/statistical word (소득세 = income tax, 소득 수준 = income level), whereas 수입 feels closer to everyday earnings, especially 한 달 수입 (monthly take). The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 'income' maps only to one fixed word and then panicking when 수입 shows up meaning 'imports' — train yourself to read the surrounding sentence. Also note 수입 is a noun describing a state (수입이 많다), so you don't conjugate it like a verb.
수입.explanation: 수입 (suip) = "income; revenue (also: imports)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 수입이 많다 ("to have a high income") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 수입, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.
수입.shortExplanation: 수입 means "income; revenue (also: imports)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
수입 is a homograph: it means both 'income' (收入) and 'imports' (輸入). Context decides — don't assume the paycheck meaning when the sentence is about trade.
Don't confuse 수입 (income/imports, 入 = enter) with 수출 (exports, 出 = exit); they are economic opposites.
For formal or statistical 'income' (income tax, income bracket) Koreans prefer 소득 (소득세, 소득 수준), not 수입.

usagePhrases.note: the opposite is 수입이 적다; describes how much money comes in
줄다 = to decrease (intransitive); 수입이 늘다 = income increases
한 달 = one month; 고정 수입 = fixed/steady income, 부수입 = side income
지출 (already in vocab) = outgo; this is the standard budgeting pair (in vs out)

examples.ko: 저는 한 달 수입이 많지 않아요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun han dal suibi manchi anayo.
examples.en: My monthly income isn't very high.
examples.note: Beginner frame: 수입이 많다/적다; 많지 않다 = not much

examples.ko: 프리랜서는 매달 수입이 일정하지 않아서 불안해요.
examples.romanization: peuriraenseoneun maedal suibi iljeonghaji anaseo buranhaeyo.
examples.en: A freelancer's income isn't steady month to month, so it's stressful.
examples.note: 일정하다 = to be steady/fixed; -지 않아서 chains the negative reason

examples.ko: 수입보다 지출이 많으면 적자가 나니까 가계부를 써 보세요.
examples.romanization: suipboda jichuri maneumyeon jeokjaga nanikka gagyebureul sseo boseyo.
examples.en: If spending exceeds income you run a deficit, so try keeping a budget book.
examples.note: 적자가 나다 = to go into the red; N보다 = than — a practical money-management line

ex.en: I decided to invest in that business.
ex.note: 기로 했어요 — a definitive financial commitment, not an on-the-spot promise

투자하다.nuance: 투자하다 is not limited to stocks or real estate. You can invest money, time, energy, or attention in a company, skill, relationship, or future goal. The resource takes 을/를 and the destination takes 에: 교육에 시간을 투자하다, 회사에 돈을 투자하다. Keep it separate from 저축하다, which means saving money for later, and 소비하다, which means spending or consuming. 투자하다 implies giving resources now because you expect future value, but the word itself does not guarantee profit or success.
투자하다.explanation: 투자하다 (tujahada) means "to invest." Build the full frame: N에 돈/시간/노력을 투자하다. The destination takes 에, and the resource being invested takes 을/를.
투자하다.shortExplanation: 투자하다 means putting money, time, or effort into something for future value.
commonMistakes: Saying 회사를 투자해요. The destination takes 에: 회사에 투자해요.
Using 투자하다 as a synonym for 저축하다. Saving cash is 저축하다; putting it into an asset or project is 투자하다.
Forgetting the invested resource: 한국어에 투자해요 can be vague. 한국어 공부에 시간을 투자해요 is clearer.
Assuming 투자 always means profit is certain. The word describes the action, not the outcome.

conjugationTips.title: 하다 verb
conjugationTips.body: 투자하다 conjugates regularly: 투자해요, 투자했어요, 투자할 거예요. A decision made in advance is often 투자하기로 했어요.

examples.ko: 저는 매달 수입의 일부만 장기 투자에 사용해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun maedal suibui ilbuman janggi tujae sayonghaeyo.
examples.en: I use only part of my monthly income for long-term investing.
examples.note: A neutral example of the financial meaning, not investment advice.

examples.ko: 요즘은 운동과 수면에 더 많은 시간을 투자하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun undonggwa sumyeone deo maneun siganeul tujahago isseoyo.
examples.en: These days, I am investing more time in exercise and sleep.
examples.note: Shows that time and health habits can also be investment targets.

examples.ko: 그 회사에 투자하기 전에 위험과 조건을 먼저 확인했어요.
examples.romanization: geu hoesae tujahagi jeone wiheomgwa jogeoneul meonjeo hwaginhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Before investing in that company, I first checked the risks and conditions.
examples.note: A careful, non-promotional financial context.

ex.en: It looks like I'll end up retiring next year.
ex.note: 게 될 것 같아요 — future form of 게 되다: circumstances will likely lead to retirement

퇴직하다.nuance: 퇴직하다 is a formal, broad verb for leaving one’s position or employment, especially in documents, company notices, benefits, and retirement contexts. 퇴사하다 specifically means leaving a company, while 은퇴하다 means retiring from an entire career or public field, and 그만두다 is the everyday ‘quit/stop.’ A person can 퇴사하다 from one company without 은퇴하다 from working life. The workplace commonly takes 에서: 회사에서 퇴직하다. 정년퇴직하다 means retiring at the official retirement age; 퇴직 후 means after leaving employment.
퇴직하다.explanation: 퇴직하다 (toejikhada) means "to retire or leave a position." It is more formal than 회사 그만두다 and broader than 퇴사하다. Choose the word by scope: one company = 퇴사하다, working career = 은퇴하다, formal employment status = 퇴직하다.
퇴직하다.shortExplanation: 퇴직하다 is a formal term for leaving employment; 퇴사하다 is leaving a company, and 은퇴하다 is retiring from a career.
commonMistakes: Using 퇴직하다 as the only translation of casual ‘I quit my job.’ In conversation, 회사 그만뒀어요 or 퇴사했어요 is often more natural.
Treating 퇴직하다 and 은퇴하다 as identical. 은퇴하다 usually ends an entire career; 퇴직하다 can mean leaving one position.
Saying 회사를 퇴직했어요 as the default. More naturally, 회사에서 퇴직했어요 or 회사를 퇴사했어요.
Confusing 퇴직금 with 월급. 퇴직금 is severance/retirement pay, not ordinary salary.

conjugationTips.title: 하다 verb
conjugationTips.body: 퇴직하다 is regular: 퇴직해요, 퇴직했어요, 퇴직할 거예요. Future circumstances are often softened as 퇴직하게 될 것 같아요.

usagePhrases.en: to retire at the mandatory retirement age
after retirement / after leaving the job
usagePhrases.note: 퇴직 functions as a noun before 후.

usagePhrases.en: to receive severance or retirement pay

examples.ko: 아버지는 올해 정년퇴직하시고 여행을 다닐 계획이에요.
examples.romanization: abeojineun olhae jeongnyeon toejikasigo yeohaengeul danil gyehoegieyo.
examples.en: My father plans to travel after retiring at the official retirement age this year.
examples.note: Honorific -시- respects the father as subject.

examples.ko: 저는 회사를 퇴사했지만 아직 은퇴한 건 아니에요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun hoesareul toesahaetjiman ajik euntoehan geon anieyo.
examples.en: I left the company, but I have not retired from working yet.
examples.note: Clearly separates 퇴사 from 은퇴.

examples.ko: 퇴직 후 건강보험과 연금 절차를 확인했어요.
examples.romanization: toejik hu geongangboheomgwa yeongeum jeolchareul hwaginhaesseoyo.
examples.en: After leaving my job, I checked the health-insurance and pension procedures.
examples.note: A realistic formal-administrative context without giving legal advice.

ex.en: I'm afraid of having to take responsibility.
ex.note: 지다 → 질까 봐: 지다 is a regular vowel-final stem, so it takes ㄹ까 봐

책임.nuance: 책임 (責任, 責 'demand/blame' + 任 'duty entrusted') is the abstract weight of being answerable for an outcome, and it lives almost entirely through verbs: 책임을 지다 (shoulder it) and 책임이 있다 (it falls on you). The dividing line you must learn is 책임 vs 의무: 책임 is accountability AFTER the fact (who answers if it goes wrong), while 의무 is a duty you are required to perform regardless of result. Also distinguish the bare noun 책임 from 책임감, which is the inner sense of duty a person feels, so describe an obligation with 책임 but a person's character with 책임감. The classic English-speaker trap is treating 책임 like the verb 'to be responsible' and saying 책임하다; Korean has no such verb, so you must reach for 책임을 지다 or 책임이 있다.
책임.explanation: 책임 (chaegim) = "responsibility". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 책임이 있다 ("to be responsible / to bear responsibility") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 책임, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
책임.shortExplanation: 책임 means "responsibility" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 책임하다 — 책임 is a noun, not a verb stem; the action is 책임을 지다 (take it) or the state is 책임이 있다.
Do not swap 책임 with 의무: 책임 is being answerable for an outcome (blame/credit), while 의무 is a duty you are required to perform.
Avoid 책임을 가지다 (a 직역 of 'have responsibility'); the natural collocation is 책임이 있다 with the subject particle 이, not 가지다.

usagePhrases.en: to be responsible / to bear responsibility
usagePhrases.note: the core stative pattern; the duty rests on you (책임이 없다 = it's not on you)
fixed phrase with 지다 (to carry on the back); this is how you say you'll own the outcome
add 감(感, feeling) to name the inner trait; describes a person, not the duty itself
add 자(者, person) for the responsible party, e.g. the manager handling an issue

examples.en: That's my responsibility.
examples.note: simplest form: 책임 + 이에요 to flatly claim a duty as yours

examples.en: Parents have a responsibility toward their children.
examples.note: N에 대한 책임 marks who or what the responsibility is for

examples.ko: 이 일은 제가 맡았으니까 끝까지 책임을 지겠습니다.
examples.romanization: i ireun jega matasseunikka kkeutkkaji chaegimeul jigetseumnida.
examples.en: Since I took on this work, I will take responsibility for it to the end.
examples.note: formal 합니다 form with 책임을 지다; common at work when committing to a task

알게 되다.en: to come to know / find out

ex.en: I found out that fact later (it came to me).
ex.note: 알다 + 게 됐어요: knowing came about through circumstances — you didn't actively seek the info, it found you

알게 되다.nuance: 알게 되다 emphasizes the process of finding out. 알다 simply states that you know.
알게 되다.explanation: 알게 되다 (alge doeda) means "to come to know; to find out". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 나중에 알게 되다 ("to find out later"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 알게 되다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
알게 되다.shortExplanation: 알게 되다 means "to come to know; to find out" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 알게 되다 when you already knew the fact all along.
Forgetting that it often pairs with a discovery trigger like 보니까, 듣고 나서, or 경험하면서.

usagePhrases.en: to come to know through experience

examples.ko: 직접 가 보니까 왜 유명한지 알게 됐어요.
examples.romanization: jikjeop ga bonikka wae yumyeonghanji alge dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: After going there myself, I found out why it is famous.
examples.note: Realization after firsthand experience.

ex.en: I decided to make a 5-year plan.
ex.note: 세우다 → 세우기로 했어요: the decision is to create the plan itself

계획.nuance: 계획(計劃, 'count/reckon + plan') is a worked-out plan or scheme for the future. Its single most important quirk is the verb: Koreans BUILD a plan with 세우다 (literally 'to erect/stand up') — 계획을 세우다 — not 만들다 ('make') as the English calque suggests. Other partners: 계획이 있다 (have a plan) and the smooth adverb 계획대로 ('as planned'). Distinguish 계획 from 예정 豫定, which is a SCHEDULED arrangement that is already set ('내일 출발할 예정이에요' = I'm scheduled/due to leave tomorrow), and from 약속, a personal commitment/appointment with someone — 계획 is your own roadmap, 예정 is a fixed scheduling, 약속 involves another party. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly 계획을 만들다 (use 세우다), and translating 'plan to do' with 계획 as a verb — Korean uses -(으)려고 하다 or -(으)ㄹ 계획이다: 여행할 계획이에요 ('I plan to travel'), not 여행을 계획해요 in casual speech.
계획.explanation: 계획 (gyehoek) = "plan". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 계획을 세워요 ("I make a plan") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 계획, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
계획.shortExplanation: 계획 means "plan" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 계획을 만들어요. The idiomatic verb is 세우다 — 계획을 세워요 (lit. 'erect a plan').
Saying 계획이 세워요 for 'I make a plan.' Making a plan is transitive — the plan is the object → 계획을 세워요.
Using 계획 for something already scheduled. 'I'm due to leave tomorrow' = 내일 떠날 예정이에요; 예정 is a fixed schedule, 계획 is a plan you draw up.

usagePhrases.note: 세우다 = set up/erect; THE verb for plans

examples.en: I'm making a travel plan.
examples.note: Simple: 계획을 세우다 — the fixed verb, lit. 'erect a plan.'

examples.en: Do you have special plans this evening?
examples.note: Everyday: 계획이 있다 — a plan exists (subject 이).

examples.en: Everything went well, just as planned.
examples.note: Real situation: 계획대로 = 'as planned,' a very natural phrase.

ex.en: Don't be too afraid of failure.
ex.note: 두려워하다 expresses fear about a noun; -(으)ㄹ까 봐 is used when the feared thing is an action/event

두려워하다.nuance: 두려워하다 means to fear a person, thing, change, or possible result. The feared target takes 을/를: 실패를 두려워하다, 변화를 두려워하다. Its adjective counterpart 두렵다 describes the state directly — 실패가 두려워요 — while 두려워하다 presents the person as showing or carrying that fear. 무섭다 is more common for something immediately scary, such as a horror movie, a threatening person, or a loud sound; 두렵다/두려워하다 often fits deeper or more abstract fears such as failure, change, and uncertainty.
두려워하다.explanation: 두려워하다 (duryeowohada) means "to fear / be afraid of." Use N을/를 두려워하다. For your immediate feeling, N이/가 두려워요 is also natural; for a concrete scary thing, 무서워요 may fit better.
두려워하다.shortExplanation: 두려워하다 takes the feared target with 을/를 and often describes deeper or abstract fear.
commonMistakes: Using 이/가 with the target in the verb frame: 실패가 두려워해요. Say 실패를 두려워해요, or use the adjective 실패가 두려워요.
Treating 무섭다 and 두려워하다 as exact synonyms. 무섭다 is common for immediate scariness; 두려워하다 often covers abstract fear.
Writing 두려워 하다 with a space. The lexical verb is one word: 두려워하다.
Adding -하다 to 무섭다 as 무서워하다 without noticing the subject perspective. 무서워하다 often describes someone showing fear; 무서워요 directly states the feeling.

conjugationTips.title: 두려워하다 vs 두렵다
conjugationTips.body: The verb is regular: 두려워해요, 두려워했어요. The adjective changes differently: 두렵다 → 두려워요. Match the particle: 실패를 두려워해요 / 실패가 두려워요.

usagePhrases.en: Do not be afraid of change.
usagePhrases.note: -지 마세요 forms a polite negative command.

usagePhrases.en: I am afraid of being alone.
usagePhrases.note: The adjective 두렵다 states the speaker’s feeling.

examples.ko: 저는 새로운 일을 시작할 때 실패를 너무 두려워하는 편이에요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun saeroun ireul sijakal ttae silpaereul neomu duryeowohaneun pyeonieyo.
examples.en: I tend to fear failure too much when I start something new.
examples.note: -는 편이다 describes a tendency.

examples.ko: 아이는 큰 소리를 무서워하지만 낯선 사람을 특별히 두려워하지는 않아요.
examples.romanization: aineun keun sorireul museowohajiman natseon sarameul teukbyeolhi duryeowohajineun anayo.
examples.en: The child is scared of loud noises but is not especially afraid of strangers.
examples.note: Contrasts immediate scariness and broader fear.

examples.ko: 결과가 두렵더라도 필요한 말은 해야 해요.
examples.romanization: gyeolgwaga duryeopdeorado piryohan mareun haeya haeyo.
examples.en: Even if the result is frightening, you need to say what is necessary.
examples.note: Uses the adjective 두렵다 with -더라도.

ex.en: I decided to summon my courage.
ex.note: 용기를 내다 (to gather courage) + 기로 했어요: even emotional decisions use 기로 하다

용기.nuance: 용기 is the Sino-Korean noun 'courage/bravery', 용기 勇氣 — 勇 'brave' + 氣 'spirit/energy' — literally 'brave spirit'. It is the positive inner strength to face fear or do something hard, a trait Koreans openly praise. The most important thing to learn is its fixed collocation: courage is something you 내다 'put out / produce', so 'work up the courage' is 용기를 내다, and the everyday imperative 용기를 내세요 means 'be brave / take heart' — using 가지다 'have' or 만들다 'make' here sounds wrong. Contrast 용기 with 자신감 (自信感) 'confidence/self-assurance': 자신감 is belief in your own ability ('confidence in your English'), built from skill, while 용기 is the nerve to act despite fear, regardless of skill. You also 얻다 'gain' or 잃다 'lose' 용기. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb choice — saying 용기를 가지다 instead of the idiomatic 용기를 내다 — and conflating 'courage' with 'confidence' (자신감), which are distinct in Korean.
용기.explanation: "courage" is 용기 (yonggi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 용기가 필요해요 ("Courage is needed"). Watch the particle attached to 용기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
용기.shortExplanation: 용기 means "courage" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 용기를 가지다 or 용기를 만들다 for 'work up courage'. The fixed idiom is 용기를 내다 ('put out courage'), e.g. 용기를 내세요.
Confusing 용기 with 자신감. 용기 is the nerve to act despite fear; 자신감 is confidence rooted in ability. 'I have 용기 in my English' should be 자신감.
Using 용기 for reckless boldness. 용기 is admirable bravery; thoughtless daring is closer to 무모함 ('recklessness'), which is negative.

usagePhrases.note: 용기 ends in a vowel → 가; 필요하다 'be needed' is the set partner
용기를 내다 'put out courage' is the fixed idiom — not 만들다 'make' or 가지다 'have'
잃다 'lose' is the opposing partner verb
북돋우다 'spur on' is the verb for giving others courage

examples.en: Be brave / Take heart
examples.note: 용기를 내다 is THE everyday phrase for 'work up the nerve'

examples.en: I worked up the courage to confess
examples.note: Verb-ㄹ/을 용기 'the courage to do' modifies 용기 with what you dared

examples.en: Your support gave me courage
examples.note: 용기를 얻다 'gain courage' pairs naturally with encouragement from others

ex.ko: 일을 하다 보니까 인맥이 생기게 됐어요.
ex.en: As I worked, I ended up building a network of connections.
ex.note: 하다 보니까 + 게 됐어요: a natural growth over time through circumstances, not planned directly

인맥.nuance: 인맥 means a network of personal connections — people you know through school, work, hobbies, or introductions who may exchange information or opportunities. It is not an internet network; that is 네트워크 or 통신망. 인맥 can be neutral or positive in 인맥이 넓다 and 인맥을 쌓다, but 인맥을 이용하다 may sound calculating if the relationship is treated only as a tool. 인연 is different: it emphasizes the meaningful connection or fate that brought people together, not the practical network itself.
인맥.explanation: 인맥 (inmaek) means "personal network / connections." Learn it with 인맥을 쌓다, 인맥이 넓다, and 인맥을 통해 알게 되다. The word describes people-links, not a technical network.
인맥.shortExplanation: 인맥 is a network of personal connections built through work, school, or social life.
commonMistakes: Using 인맥 for Wi-Fi or computer networks. Use 네트워크 or 통신망 for technical networks.
Assuming 인맥 always has a negative ‘connections and favoritism’ meaning. It can simply mean one’s professional or social network.
Saying 인맥이 많다 as the only pattern. 인맥이 넓다 is the common way to say someone is well connected.
Confusing 인맥 with 인연. 인맥 is a practical network; 인연 is a meaningful personal connection or bond.

usagePhrases.note: 쌓다 presents connections as accumulated over time.
The fixed descriptive collocation uses 넓다.

usagePhrases.en: to come to know someone through one’s network

examples.ko: 행사에 자주 참여하다 보니 자연스럽게 인맥이 넓어졌어요.
examples.romanization: haengsae jaju chamyeohada boni jayeonseureopge inmaegi neolbeojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: As I kept attending events, my network naturally grew.
examples.note: The network develops as a result, not necessarily as a calculated goal.

examples.ko: 그 회사 담당자를 친구의 인맥을 통해 소개받았어요.
examples.romanization: geu hoesa damdangjareul chinguui inmaegeul tonghae sogaebadasseoyo.
examples.en: I was introduced to the person in charge at that company through a friend’s connections.
examples.note: A neutral professional introduction through a personal network.

examples.ko: 인맥만 믿기보다 실력과 신뢰를 같이 쌓는 게 중요해요.
examples.romanization: inmaengman mitgiboda sillyeokgwa silloereul gachi ssanneun ge jungyohaeyo.
examples.en: Rather than relying only on connections, it is important to build skill and trust as well.
examples.note: Shows the potentially instrumental side without treating the word itself as negative.

감동.en: deep emotion; being moved or touched

ex.ko: 그 영화 너무 감동적이어서 울 뻔했어요.
ex.en: That movie was so moving I almost cried.
ex.note: 감동적이다 = to be moving/touching; 울 뻔했어요 shows the emotional near-miss naturally

감동.nuance: 감동 is the warm, welling-up feeling of being moved or touched — the lump-in-the-throat reaction to a kind gesture, a film, or a reunion. It is Sino-Korean, 感動 ('feel' 感 + 'move/stir' 動), literally 'the heart being moved', which is exactly the English metaphor 'to be moved', so the image transfers nicely. The key learner difficulty is the verb frames: Korean splits 'being moved' (감동을 받다, 'receive emotion') from 'moving others' (감동을 주다, 'give emotion'), and the standalone verb 감동하다/감동받다 means YOU felt it — never 'to move a physical object' (that is 옮기다 or 움직이다). Compare the near-synonym 인상 印象 (impression): 인상 깊다 ('it left a deep impression') is more neutral and cognitive, while 감동 is purely emotional and positive. Compare also 감격 (overwhelming emotion, often tears) which is stronger and rarer. Natural collocations: 감동을 받다/주다, 큰 감동 (not 많은 감동), 감동적인 N. Tone is sincere and a touch earnest; the slang 감동 먹다 is friendly but casual only.
감동.explanation: 감동 (gamdong) means "deep emotion; being moved/touched". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 감동을 받다 ("to be moved/touched"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 감동 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
감동.shortExplanation: 감동 means "deep emotion; being moved/touched" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 감동하다 like English 'to move (an object)': 책상을 감동했어요 is wrong — for moving things use 옮기다 (relocate) or 움직이다 (budge). 감동하다 only means a person was emotionally moved.
Saying 많은 감동 for 'a lot of emotion'. Korean counts this feeling by size, not amount, so the natural phrase is 큰 감동 (great/deep emotion). 많은 감동 sounds off.
Mixing up who feels it: using 감동을 줬어요 when you mean YOU were touched. 주다 = give (you moved others); to say you yourself were moved, use 감동을 받았어요 or 감동했어요.

usagePhrases.note: 감동 + 을 받다; the standard way to say YOU were moved — literally 'to receive emotion'. This is the most common form.
감동 + 을 주다; literally 'to give emotion' — used when a film, person, or story moves others
감동 + 적이다 makes the adjective; modifier form 감동적인 영화 (a moving film)
casual/slang; 감동 먹었어 = 'I was so touched' among friends — never in formal writing

examples.en: That movie was really moving.
examples.note: Simplest frame: 감동이다 used directly as 'was moving'. Casual-polite 요-speech, the most natural quick reaction.

examples.en: I read grandma's letter and was moved.
examples.note: Everyday frame: 감동을 받다 = the experiencer was touched. Note 을 받다 ('receive'), not 했다 — this is how Korean frames being moved.

examples.ko: 선수의 마지막 인사가 모든 사람에게 큰 감동을 줬어요.
examples.romanization: seonsuui majimak insaga modeun saramege keun gamdongeul jwosseoyo.
examples.en: The athlete's final farewell gave everyone deep emotion.
examples.note: Real-situation: 감동을 주다 (give emotion) flips the viewpoint to the SOURCE. 큰 감동 (great emotion) is the natural collocation, not 많은 감동.

ex.ko: 그 사람 표정을 보니까 많이 두려워하나 봐요.
ex.en: From that person's expression, I guess they're really afraid.
ex.note: 두려워하다 is an action verb, so it takes -나 봐요. The visible expression is the evidence.

두려움.nuance: 두려움 is the noun 'fear/dread', from the adjective 두렵다 (a ㅂ-irregular: 두렵 + 음 → 두려움). It names a deep, often anticipatory inner fear — of the future, failure, the unknown — more reflective and lasting than a sudden jolt. Separate two relatives: 무서움/무섭다 is concrete, gut-level scared ('a scary movie', 'the dog is scary'), the word you actually say in conversation, whereas 두려움 is heavier, more abstract and literary, and is the one paired with big life anxieties. A third, 공포 (恐怖), is sheer terror/horror, the genre word for horror films and panic. So a spider triggers 무서움, an uncertain future triggers 두려움, a horror movie deals in 공포. The English-speaker pitfall: 'fear' maps to all of these, so beginners overuse 두려움 in casual speech where 무서워요 is natural, and forget the ㅂ-irregular spelling (두렵다 → 두려워요, 두려움).
두려움.explanation: 두려움 (duryeoum) = "fear". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 두려움이 밀려와요 ("Fear washes over me") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 두려움, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
두려움.shortExplanation: 두려움 means "fear" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 두려움이에요 for 'I'm scared'. That means 'It is fear'. Use the adjective 무서워요 (everyday) or 두려워요 (weightier).
Overusing 두려움 for concrete scares. A scary dog or movie is 무섭다/공포, not 두려움, which suits abstract dread (실패에 대한 두려움 'fear of failure').
Mis-conjugating the ㅂ-irregular: 두렵다 becomes 두려워요 and the noun is 두려움 — not '두렵음'. The ㅂ softens to 우 before a vowel.

usagePhrases.note: 두려움 + 이; 밀려오다 conveys fear creeping or surging in
느끼다 'feel' is the standard verb for this inner emotion
이겨내다 'win out over' is the inspiring partner verb
noun + 없이 'without' is the set adverbial phrase

examples.en: I'm scared to sleep alone
examples.note: for plain 'I'm scared' use the adjective 무섭다, not the noun 두려움

examples.en: I felt fear before a new challenge
examples.note: 앞에서 'in front of' frames what you face; 두려움 fits abstract dread

examples.ko: 실패에 대한 두려움이 그를 멈추게 했어요
examples.romanization: silpaee daehan duryeoumi geureul meomchuge haesseoyo
examples.en: Fear of failure made him stop
examples.note: N에 대한 두려움 'fear of/about N' is the standard frame for what is feared

ex.ko: 팀장님 말투가 그러는 걸 보니까 화나신 건가 봐요.
ex.en: The way the team leader is talking, I'm guessing they're angry.
ex.note: -(으)ㄴ가 봐요 = inferring the emotion from observable evidence (their tone)

분노.nuance: 분노 is the Sino-Korean noun for 'anger/wrath', 분노 憤怒 — 憤 'indignation' + 怒 'rage' — so by its very characters it is righteous, intense fury, not petty annoyance. The crucial contrast for learners is the everyday word 화 (火, literally 'fire'): in conversation Koreans say 화가 나다 'anger arises' or 화를 내다 'show anger' for ordinary irritation, while 분노 is reserved for grave, often moral or collective rage — social injustice, betrayal, public outrage — and shows up in news, speeches, and writing far more than in casual chat. Saying 분노했어요 over a late bus sounds comically overblown; 짜증 났어요 'I got annoyed' or 화가 났어요 fits. The pitfall: English 'angry' is one word covering all intensities, so learners overuse 분노. Match the register — keep 분노 for the heavy stuff and use 화/짜증 for daily friction.
분노.explanation: "anger" is 분노 (bunno). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 분노가 치밀다 ("anger surges up"). Watch the particle attached to 분노 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
분노.shortExplanation: 분노 means "anger" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 분노 for everyday irritation. 분노 is grave wrath (often moral/public). For 'I'm annoyed/angry' in daily life, say 화가 났어요 or 짜증 났어요.
Treating 분노 like an adjective: 분노해요 to mean 'I'm angry' is stiff. Either use the verb 분노하다 only for serious outrage, or switch to 화가 나요.
Mismatched verb: 분노를 하다 is wrong. Use 분노를 느끼다 'feel anger', 분노가 치밀다 'anger surges', or 분노하다 as one verb.

usagePhrases.note: 분노 + 가; 치밀다 'boil/well up' is the set verb for rising rage
느끼다 'feel' is the neutral verb for the emotion
참다 'endure/suppress' is the habitual partner for restraining 분노
분노 + 의 + noun links the feeling to what shows it

examples.en: I'm so angry
examples.note: in daily speech the everyday phrase is 화가 나다, not the heavy noun 분노

examples.en: I felt anger at the unfair ruling
examples.note: 에 marks the trigger; 분노 suits weighty, public injustices

examples.en: The citizens' anger burst out into the streets
examples.note: this grave, news-style register is exactly where 분노 belongs

ex.ko: 합격했다는 소식을 듣고 만족스러워서 소리를 지를 뻔했어요.
ex.en: When I heard I passed, I was so satisfied I almost shouted.
ex.note: 만족스럽다 = to feel satisfied; 소리를 지르다 = to shout; 지를 뻔했어요 = almost-shouted close call

만족.nuance: 만족 (滿足, 滿 'full' + 足 'enough/sufficient') is literally being 'filled to sufficiency' — the settled feeling that something has met or exceeded your expectations. The synonym line to hold: 만족 is being content with what you have, whereas 행복 is broad life-happiness and 만끽(滿喫) is actively savoring something to the full — you 만족하다 with a meal's quality but 만끽하다 the flavor moment by moment. Register is neutral and everyday; 만족하다 names the person's state, 만족스럽다 calls the thing satisfying. English-speaker pitfall: 'satisfied WITH' makes English speakers write N을 만족하다, but the particle is 에 — 결과에 만족하다, never 결과를 만족하다. Also resist 만족하다 for an object's quality ('the result is satisfying' = 결과가 만족스럽다, not 결과가 만족하다).
만족.explanation: 만족 (manjok) means "satisfaction; contentment". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 만족하다 ("to be satisfied"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 만족 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
만족.shortExplanation: 만족 means "satisfaction; contentment" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Wrong particle from English 'satisfied with': it is N에 만족하다 (서비스에 만족해요), not N을/를 만족하다
Using 만족하다 to describe a thing: 'the result is satisfying' is 결과가 만족스러워요, while 만족하다 describes the satisfied person
Confusing 만족 (being content with) with 만끽 (savoring/enjoying to the full) — they share the 滿 but 만끽 is active relishing, not quiet contentment

usagePhrases.note: 보통 N에 만족하다 — note the particle 에, not 을/를
adjective describing the result: 만족스러운 결과
度 'degree'; common in reviews and surveys, 만족도가 높다
大 'big'; casual emphatic, 가격 대비 대만족이에요

examples.en: If it's this much, I'm satisfied.
examples.note: 만족하다 stands alone as a state of contentment

examples.ko: 새로 산 노트북 성능에 아주 만족해요.
examples.romanization: saero san noteubuk seongneunge aju manjokaeyo.
examples.en: I'm very satisfied with the performance of the laptop I just bought.
examples.note: the thing you're satisfied with takes 에: 성능에 만족하다

examples.ko: 이번 여행은 날씨도 좋고 음식도 맛있어서 정말 만족스러웠어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon yeohaengeun nalssido joko eumsikdo masisseoseo jeongmal manjokseureowosseoyo.
examples.en: This trip was truly satisfying because the weather was nice and the food was good.
examples.note: describe the experience itself with 만족스럽다

ex.ko: 그분이 모르는 척한 것 때문에 신뢰를 잃었어요.
ex.en: Because he pretended not to know, I lost trust in him.
ex.note: 모르는 척하다 (pretending not to know) combined with 신뢰를 잃다 (lose trust) — common real-life pairing

신뢰.nuance: 신뢰 (信賴, 信 'believe' + 賴 'rely on') is trust as a reasoned, earned noun — more formal and weighty than the everyday verb 믿다 (to believe/trust someone in the moment). The key contrast for learners is 신뢰 vs 믿음: 믿음 leans emotional or even religious (faith), while 신뢰 is confidence built on a track record, which is why it fits people, workplaces, and institutions alike. You say 신뢰가 가다 ('trust flows') when someone earns your confidence and 신뢰가 무너지다 when it shatters. Note that unlike 우정, 신뢰 does take 하다: 신뢰하다 means 'to trust (someone),' taking the person as a 을/를 object. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 믿다 in formal writing where Korean prefers the noun 신뢰 (e.g. 신뢰를 쌓다, not 믿음을 만들다).
신뢰.explanation: "trust" is 신뢰 (silloe). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 신뢰가 가다 ("to feel trust toward someone"). Watch the particle attached to 신뢰 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
신뢰.shortExplanation: 신뢰 means "trust" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 신뢰 as only a noun — 신뢰하다 is a valid verb (저는 그를 신뢰해요); choose noun or verb by register
Confusing 신뢰 (earned, reasoned trust) with 믿음 (belief/faith), which is more emotional or religious
Saying 신뢰를 만들다 (make trust) — use 신뢰를 쌓다 (build up); trust is accumulated, not manufactured

usagePhrases.note: 신뢰가 가다 (trust flows/comes) is the everyday way to say 'I find them trustworthy'
쌓다 (pile up) — trust is accumulated over repeated reliable actions, never made overnight
잃다 = lose; the result of a broken promise or a lie
무너지다 = crumble/collapse, a stronger total breakdown than just 잃다

examples.en: I trust that person.
examples.note: 신뢰하다 as a verb takes the person as object with 을/를, sounding considered and formal

examples.ko: 저 사람은 말한 건 꼭 지켜서 신뢰가 가.
examples.romanization: jeo sarameun malhan geon kkok jikyeoseo silloega ga.
examples.en: That person always keeps their word, so I trust them.
examples.note: 지키다 = keep (a promise); 신뢰가 가 is the natural banmal verdict on someone

examples.ko: 회사에서 신뢰를 쌓으려면 오랜 시간이 걸려요.
examples.romanization: hoesaeseo silloereul ssaeuryeomyeon oraen sigani geollyeoyo.
examples.en: Building trust at work takes a long time.
examples.note: -(으)려면 = if you want to; pairs with 쌓다 to stress trust as slow accumulation

ex.ko: 그분 이야기가 나오면 다들 조용해지는 걸 보니까 많이 존경하나 봐요.
ex.en: Seeing everyone quiet down when that person comes up, I guess they respect them a lot.
ex.note: 존경하다 is an action verb, so it takes -나 봐요. The group reaction gives the clue.

존경.nuance: 존경 (尊敬, 尊 'revere/honor' + 敬 'respect') stacks two reverence characters into deep admiration for a person's character, effort, or achievement — stronger than mere 인정(認定) 'acknowledgment.' The synonym line every learner needs: 존경 is looking UP to a person, while 존중(尊重) is respecting someone's rights, opinions or choices on equal terms — you 존경하다 a mentor you admire, but 존중하다 a colleague's differing view. Register: formal and warm; you'll hear 존경하는 before a title in speeches and letters, and 존경받는 사람 is high praise. English-speaker pitfall: English 'respect' covers both senses, so learners say 존경 when they mean 존중 (e.g. 'I respect your decision' must be 존중해요, not 존경해요). Also keep 존경 for people — to 'respect/value' an abstract thing like time or rules, use 중요하게 여기다 or 존중하다, not 존경하다.
존경.explanation: "respect; admiration (for someone)" is 존경 (jongyeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 존경하다 ("to respect / look up to"). Watch the particle attached to 존경 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
존경.shortExplanation: 존경 means "respect; admiration (for someone)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 존경 where 존중 is meant: 'I respect your opinion/decision' is 존중해요 (equal-footing respect), not 존경해요 (looking up to a person)
Applying 존경 to objects or ideas; it targets people you admire, so for valuing a thing use 중요하게 여기다
Confusing it with 인정(認定) 'acknowledgment'; 인정하다 is granting that someone is good, while 존경하다 is heartfelt admiration that goes further

usagePhrases.note: 존경하는 선생님 = a teacher I look up to
passive; 존경받는 사람 = a respected person, high praise
心 'heart'; the inner sentiment, 존경심을 가지다/느끼다
adjective; 정말 존경스러워요 = I truly admire (that)

examples.en: I truly respect that person.
examples.note: 존경하다 takes a person as its direct object

examples.ko: 힘든 일을 묵묵히 해내는 부모님께 존경심을 느껴요.
examples.romanization: himdeun ireul mungmuki haenaeneun bumonimkke jongyeongsimeul neukkyeoyo.
examples.en: I feel respect for my parents, who quietly get hard things done.
examples.note: 존경심을 느끼다, with 께 honoring the elders

examples.en: That professor is someone respected by the students.
examples.note: 존경받다 with 에게 marking who does the respecting

ex.en: That person seems really diligent.
ex.note: 성실하다 is an adjective → 성실한 것 같다 (soft opinion); contrast with -나 보다 which implies outside evidence

성실하다.nuance: 성실하다 (誠實하다, from 誠 'sincerity' + 實 'substance/truth') is one of the most valued character words in Korean work and school culture: it means earnest, diligent, and reliable in carrying out duties — the steady person who shows up and follows through. Because it praises consistent effort rather than results, it is the single safest strength to claim in an interview ('저는 성실합니다'). The key near-synonym to separate is 정직하다 (honest): 성실 is about diligence and faithfulness to your work, while 정직 is about not lying — a lazy person can still be 정직, and a liar can technically be 성실. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: do not double the 하 (the 요-form is 성실해요, never 성실하해요), and do not reach for 성실하다 when you mean 'sincere' in the sense of heartfelt feelings — that emotional sincerity is 진실하다 or 진심이다; 성실 is sincerity expressed as hard work.
성실하다.explanation: "sincere, diligent, conscientious" is 성실하다 (seongsilhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 성실한 사람 ("a diligent, dependable person"). Watch the particle attached to 성실하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
성실하다.shortExplanation: 성실하다 means "sincere, diligent, conscientious" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 성실하해요: the stem already ends in 하다, so it conjugates 성실해요 / 성실한 — only one 해
Using it for 'honest' (doesn't lie): that overlapping-but-different idea is 정직하다; 성실 is about diligence/reliability
Using it for heartfelt 'sincere' (a sincere apology): that emotional sincerity is 진심으로/진실하다, not 성실하다

usagePhrases.note: Top-tier compliment for a worker or student; pairs with the noun directly via the -ㄴ form
성실하게 = adverb form; the habitual partner is 일하다 or 공부하다, framing steady effort
태도 (attitude) is praised more than raw talent in Korean work culture
성실히 = slightly more formal -히 adverb; 임하다 (to undertake) is written/formal register

examples.en: That friend is truly diligent and dependable.
examples.note: Simplest frame: 성실하다 + 요-ending; note the stem 하 becomes 해요

examples.ko: 저는 무슨 일이든 성실하게 하려고 노력해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun museun irideun seongsilhage haryeogo noryeokaeyo.
examples.en: I try to do everything diligently, whatever the task.
examples.note: Everyday self-PR line for interviews; 무슨 일이든 = whatever the task; adverb 성실하게 modifies 하다

examples.en: We gave a scholarship to the student who attended faithfully.
examples.note: Real situation: 출석하다 = attend; here 성실 covers showing up consistently over a term

ex.ko: 그 사람이 사실대로 말하는 걸 보니까 정직한 사람인가 봐요.
ex.en: Seeing that person tell the truth, I guess they're an honest person.
ex.note: 정직한 사람인가 봐요 uses noun phrase 사람인가 봐요 after the adjective modifier 정직한.

정직하다.nuance: 정직하다 (正直하다, 正 'correct/upright' + 直 'straight') means honest and truthful in the moral sense: not lying, not cheating, dealing straight with people. The near-synonym you must distinguish is 솔직하다 (率直, frank/candid): 솔직하다 is about openly saying what you really think or feel ('솔직히 말하면…' = to be frank…), whereas 정직하다 is about not deceiving anyone — a moral judgment, not a communication style. You praise a child, a clerk, or a business as 정직하다; you call someone 솔직하다 when they bluntly share an opinion. Register: 정직하다 is a weighty ethical compliment, while 솔직하다 is everyday and can even be a mild warning ('너무 솔직해' = a bit too blunt). The English-speaker pitfall is mapping both English 'honest' senses onto one word — in 'Honestly, I think…' English 'honestly' means 솔직히, not 정직히. Also, 정직해 보이다 means 'seems honest/trustworthy,' not 'looks smart.'
정직하다.explanation: 정직하다 (jeongjikada) = "honest, truthful, upright". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 정직한 사람 ("an honest, upright person") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 정직하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
정직하다.shortExplanation: 정직하다 means "honest, truthful, upright" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 정직하다 (honest, doesn't lie — a moral trait) with 솔직하다 (frank, openly says what they feel — a style)
Translating the discourse marker 'Honestly, …' as 정직히: it should be 솔직히 말하면 / 솔직히
Reading 정직해 보이다 as 'looks smart'; it means 'seems honest/trustworthy'

usagePhrases.note: Moral praise; implies they don't lie or cheat, a deeper claim than mere friendliness
정직하게 = adverb; very often paired with owning up to a mistake or telling an uncomfortable truth
Set phrase about leading an upright, above-board life — a moral self-image
Proverb-style saying taught in school; 정직이 takes the subject particle 이

examples.en: That person is very honest.
examples.note: Plain frame; 정직하다 → 정직해요, a flat moral judgment about character

examples.ko: 실수했을 때 정직하게 말하는 게 제일 중요해요.
examples.romanization: silsuhaesseul ttae jeongjikage malhaneun ge jeil jungyohaeyo.
examples.en: When you make a mistake, being honest about it is the most important thing.
examples.note: Everyday work advice; 실수 = mistake; 정직하게 말하다 = come clean rather than cover up

examples.ko: 그 가게는 30년 동안 정직하게 장사해서 단골이 많아요.
examples.romanization: geu gageneun 30nyeon dongan jeongjikage jangsahaeseo dangori manayo.
examples.en: That shop has done business honestly for 30 years, so it has many regulars.
examples.note: Real situation: 정직 applied to a business — no overcharging or cheating; 단골 = regular customer

신중하다.en: to be careful; prudent; cautious in decisions

ex.ko: 그 사람 말을 잘 안 하는 걸 보니까 신중한가 봐요.
ex.en: They don't say much — I'm guessing they're the careful type.
ex.note: 신중하다 → -(으)ㄴ가 봐요; inferring personality from observable behavior

신중하다.nuance: 신중하다 (愼重하다, 愼 'careful/prudent' + 重 'weighty/grave') means prudent and careful specifically about decisions and words — weighing things seriously before you act or speak, rather than rushing. It is the polished, positive way to describe caution, and a great interview strength (the mature flip side of being slow). Crucially, separate it from two look-alikes: 조심하다 is physical 'be careful / watch out' (조심하세요 = mind the step, take care on the road), so you never use 신중하다 for bodily caution; and 소심하다 is fearful timidity. 신중하다 is thoughtful deliberation, neither physical wariness nor anxiety. Its negative twin is 우유부단하다 (indecisive): 신중하다 weighs wisely and then chooses, while 우유부단 just can't choose. Register: fully positive and usable formally (신중을 기하다 in notices). The English-speaker pitfall is using 신중하다 like English 'careful' for everything — 'be careful with the knife' is 칼 조심하세요, not 신중. Stem note: 신중해요, not 신중하해요.
신중하다.explanation: "prudent, careful, cautious (in decisions)" is 신중하다 (sinjunghada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 신중한 사람 ("a prudent, careful person"). Watch the particle attached to 신중하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
신중하다.shortExplanation: 신중하다 means "prudent, careful, cautious (in decisions)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 신중하다 for physical 'be careful' (watch the steps, mind the hot pan) — that is 조심하다
Saying 신중하해요: the 하다 stem yields 신중해요 / 신중한
Blurring it with 우유부단하다: 신중하다 deliberates then decides; 우유부단하다 is the failure to decide at all

usagePhrases.note: Compliment for someone who thinks before acting or speaking
신중하게 = adverb; the textbook partners are 결정하다 (decide) and 선택하다 (choose)
Often advised before a big, irreversible choice
Formal set phrase (기하다 = 'aim for'); common in announcements and official notices

examples.en: That person makes decisions carefully.
examples.note: Simple frame pairing the adverb 신중하게 with its core partner 결정하다

examples.ko: 큰돈이 들어가는 일이라 신중하게 결정해야 해요.
examples.romanization: keundoni deureoganeun irira sinjunghage gyeoljeonghaeya haeyo.
examples.en: It involves a lot of money, so we have to decide carefully.
examples.note: Everyday practical use for contracts or real estate; 큰돈 = a large sum; -아/어야 하다 = have to

examples.en: Think it over carefully before you decide to change jobs.
examples.note: Real situation: -고 나서 = after doing; 이직 = changing jobs — a weighty life choice

냉정하다.en: to be coolheaded; level-headed; cold; detached

ex.en: I pretended to be coolheaded, but it was actually hard.
ex.note: 냉정한 척하다 uses the target adjective directly: acting detached even when you are shaken inside.

냉정하다.nuance: 냉정하다 (冷靜하다, 冷 'cold' + 靜 'quiet/calm') is two-faced and context decides everything.
