그다음.shortExplanation: 그다음 means "then; after that; next" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 그다음 as a noun for 'the next person' unless the context is clear.
For immediate timing, use -자마자 or 바로, not only 그다음.

usagePhrases.note: Useful when asking about the next step.

usagePhrases.en: First I wash, and then I eat breakfast.
usagePhrases.note: 먼저 and 그다음 make the sequence easy to follow.

examples.ko: 예약을 확인하고 나서 그다음 방으로 올라갔어요.
examples.romanization: yeyageul hwaginhago naseo geudaeum bangeuro ollagasseoyo.
examples.en: After checking the reservation, I went up to the room next.
examples.note: 그다음 names the following step after a completed action.

ex.en: After getting ready, I left right away.
ex.note: 바로 pairs naturally with sequence sentences.

바로.nuance: 바로 carries two everyday senses split by context: 'right away / immediately' with actions (바로 가요, 바로 출발해요) and 'exactly / right (there)' with places and identifications (바로 여기, 바로 앞, 바로 그거예요). For the time sense, its near-synonym 곧 means 'soon / shortly' — a small gap remains — while 바로 means truly 'this instant, with zero delay', so 바로 가요 is more immediate than 곧 가요. For the location/identification sense, 바로 tightens 'next to/in front of' into 'directly, precisely' and has no single English twin; it behaves like 'right' in 'right next to'. It collocates tightly with position words (바로 옆/앞/뒤/위) and with emphatic confirmations (바로 그거, 바로 너 'you, exactly'). The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 바로 only means 'immediately' and missing its 'exactly/right-there' use, plus stranding it from the word it marks — keep 바로 hugging the verb or noun (바로 앞, not 앞 바로).
바로.explanation: "right away; exactly, right (there)" is 바로 (baro). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 바로 가요 ("I'll go right away"). Watch the particle attached to 바로 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
바로.shortExplanation: 바로 means "right away; exactly, right (there)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 바로 only means 'immediately': it equally means 'exactly/right (there)' for places and things, as in 바로 여기 and 바로 그거예요.
Separating 바로 from the word it modifies: it must hug the verb or noun — 바로 앞, not 앞 바로; 바로 가요, not 가요 바로.
Swapping 바로 and 곧 for the time sense: 바로 가요 ('go this instant') is more immediate than 곧 가요 ('go soon'), which leaves a short gap.

usagePhrases.note: The time sense: immediately, with no delay
The location sense: points to an exact spot
바로 앞에 있어요 = it's right in front; 바로 pins the position

examples.en: I'll go right now.
examples.note: 지금 바로 = right this very moment, no waiting

examples.en: The school is right next to my house.
examples.note: 바로 옆 = directly beside

examples.en: Let's leave right away.
examples.note: 바로 before the verb signals immediacy

ex.en: I just arrived.
ex.note: Recent completion, not necessarily immediate sequence.

방금.nuance: 방금 (方今, 方 'just/at the time' + 今 'now') is the tightest 'recent past' word, pointing to something that happened only seconds to a couple of minutes ago. The contrast learners need most is 방금 vs 아까: 방금 is 'this very moment past,' while 아까 stretches to 'earlier today' (potentially hours back). 방금 나갔어요 = 'they left seconds ago'; 아까 나갔어요 = 'they left a while ago.' Compare also 방금 vs 막: both can mean 'just now,' but 막 emphasizes the instantaneous edge ('right as it happened') and pairs with 지금/참이다, whereas 방금 is a standalone time word and a touch more neutral. Because of its Sino-Korean root, the variant 방금 전(에) ('just a moment before') is common. 방금 is strictly immediate past — never future. Register is neutral and fits both casual and polite speech, which is why staff use it (방금 주문하신…).
방금.explanation: "just now, a moment ago (seconds)" is 방금 (banggeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 방금 도착하다 ("to have just arrived"). Watch the particle attached to 방금 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
방금.shortExplanation: 방금 means "just now, a moment ago (seconds)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Stretching it to hours ago: for 'earlier today' use 아까. 방금 means only seconds to a couple minutes back.
Using it for the future: 방금 is strictly the immediate past, never 'in a moment' — that's 곧 / 이따가.
Over-distinguishing from 막 when they overlap: in many sentences 방금 도착했어요 and (지금) 막 도착했어요 are interchangeable, but pick 막 when you want the 'right as it happened' edge.

usagePhrases.note: 방금 도착했어요 = I got here only seconds ago
방금 뭐라고 했어요? = asking to repeat what was said a second ago
Common variant emphasizing the very recent instant
방금까지 여기 있었어요 = it was right here until seconds ago

examples.en: I arrived just now.
examples.note: Simple: 방금 + past for an action seconds old

examples.en: The drink you just ordered is ready.
examples.note: Everyday: 방금 in a cafe, an order only moments old, polite -습니다 register

examples.ko: 방금까지 옆에 있었는데 잠깐 사이에 어디 갔지?
examples.romanization: banggeumkkaji yeope isseonneunde jamkkan saie eodi gatji?
examples.en: They were right beside me until just now; where'd they go in that instant?
examples.note: Real situation: 방금까지 emphasizing 'up until seconds ago'

cluster.title: 이제 vs 지금 vs 방금 vs 아까
cluster.rule: 지금 just points at this exact moment, while 이제 says the situation has changed ("now, unlike before"). The two past ones split purely by depth: 방금 is seconds to a couple of minutes ago, 아까 is earlier today.

example.en: What are you doing right now?

members.hint: "a second ago" — the tightest recent past

ex.en: After washing my hands, I eat.
ex.note: A textbook-clear completion sequence.

씻다.nuance: 씻다 means to wash with water and, despite the tense-looking ㅅ, is a perfectly regular verb: the ㅅ stays in every form, giving 씻어요, 씻었어요, 씻습니다 (the ㅅ never drops the way it does in true ㅅ-irregular verbs like 짓다→지어요). It covers washing hands, face, body, and rinsing food. Korean, however, distributes 'wash/clean' across several verbs you must keep apart: 씻다 is for rinsing body parts and food; 감다 is reserved for washing hair (머리를 감다, never 머리를 씻다); 닦다 is 'wipe/scrub/polish' and is what you use for brushing teeth (이를 닦다) and wiping surfaces; and 빨다 is for washing laundry (빨래를 빨다), often replaced by 세탁하다 for machine washing 빨래하다. The whole-body version is 씻다 generically, or the Sino-Korean 샤워하다 'shower'. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'wash' is one word, so learners say 머리를 씻다 for 'wash my hair' (wrong → 감다) or 이를 씻다 for 'brush teeth' (wrong → 닦다).
씻다.explanation: 씻다 (ssitda) = "to wash". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 씻어요 plus one useful sentence like 손을 씻어요 ("I wash my hands"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 씻고 싶어요 for what you want, 씻을 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 씻어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
씻다.shortExplanation: 씻다 means "to wash" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 씻다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 씻어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 씻다 for hair — washing hair has its own verb 감다, so 'I wash my hair' is 머리를 감아요, not 머리를 씻어요.
Using 씻다 for teeth — brushing teeth is 이를 닦다 (a wiping/scrubbing action), so it must be 이를 닦아요, not 이를 씻어요.
Dropping the ㅅ like an irregular verb (씨어요) — 씻다 is regular, so the ㅅ stays: 씻어요, 씻었어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 씻다 becomes 씻을 수 있어요 ("can") and 씻을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: body parts you wash take 을/를

examples.en: I wash my hands before eating.
examples.note: habit; 손을 씻다 fixed collocation

examples.en: I wash my face with cold water every morning.
examples.note: with-instrument 찬물로; 씻어요 regular

examples.en: Wash the strawberries clean under running water.
examples.note: 씻으세요 with 으 before the honorific after a consonant stem

ex.en: After grabbing my wallet, I left.
ex.note: The departure waits until the previous step is complete.

출발하다.nuance: 출발하다 is Sino-Korean 出發(출발: 出 go out + 發 set off/shoot) plus 하다, the crisp word for a journey or vehicle SETTING OFF from a starting line. Contrast it with 떠나다(leave): 출발하다 is neutral and logistical, fixed on the departure point and time (기차가 출발하다), so a station announcer uses it; 떠나다 carries the emotional weight of leaving something or someone behind. The starting place takes 에서 (부산에서 출발해요) and the time takes 에 (3시에 출발해요). Because it's a 하다 verb the stem 하 + 아 fuses to 해, so present is 출발해요 and the negative splits as 출발 안 해요. English-speaker pitfall: don't mark the start point with 에 — you depart FROM somewhere, so it's 공항에서 출발해요, and the opposite endpoint verb is 도착하다.
출발하다.explanation: "to depart" in Korean is 출발하다 (chulbalhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 출발해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 출발하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 기차가 곧 출발해요 ("The train departs soon.") — then reshape the same stem into 출발하고 싶어요 (desire), 출발할 수 있어요 (ability), and 출발 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
출발하다.shortExplanation: 출발하다 means "to depart" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 출발하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 출발해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the starting place with 에 (공항에 출발해요). The origin you leave from takes 에서; 에 would point at a destination, which belongs to 도착하다.
Saying 출발하지 않아요 / 출발해 안 해요 awkwardly — the clean short negative of a 하다 verb is 출발 안 해요, splitting the noun from 해요.
Treating it as emotional 'leave' for people (친구를 출발했어요). To leave a person or place behind you need 떠나다; 출발하다 is for setting off on a route or schedule.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 출발하다 becomes 출발할 수 있어요 ("can") and 출발할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

examples.en: Let's set off now!
examples.note: 출발 + 하다, and 하 + 아 always fuses to 해, giving 출발해요.

examples.en: The bus leaves at 9, so we'd better hurry.
examples.note: 니까 gives the reason; time of departure takes 에.

examples.en: Even if it rains, we'll depart as planned.
examples.note: 아도 = even if; 예정대로 = as scheduled.

cluster.title: 시작하다 vs 출발하다
cluster.rule: English "start" covers both, but Korean never mixes them: 시작하다 is an activity beginning (class, work, a movie), 출발하다 is a person or vehicle physically leaving the starting point. You can 출발하다 for school and 시작하다 the class after you arrive.

members.hint: physically setting off from a place

챙기다.en: to grab; to pack; to take care of

ex.en: After grabbing my wallet, I left.
ex.note: A common pre-departure action.

챙기다.nuance: 챙기다 is one of the most useful 'caring' verbs in daily Korean, with a cluster of related senses: (1) gather/pack the things you need (짐을 챙기다), (2) make sure not to skip something, especially food (밥 챙겨 먹어 'make sure you eat'), and (3) look after a person attentively (동생 좀 챙겨 'keep an eye on your sibling'). Set it against 돌보다 (care for over time, like nursing a child or the sick): 챙기다 is quicker, more about 'making sure / not letting slip', while 돌보다 is sustained nurturing. It also contrasts with 챙겨 주다, where adding 주다 makes the care explicitly a favour for someone. The English trap is reaching for 들다 'lift' or 가지다 'have' when you mean 'grab/remember to bring' — that everyday act is 챙기다. Native warmth: 잘 챙겨 먹어요 is a standard way to say 'take care of yourself'.
챙기다.explanation: 챙기다 (chaenggida) means "to take care of". Start from the polite form 챙겨요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 챙기다. A strong first sentence is 짐을 챙기다 ("to pack/gather one's things"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 챙기다 also becomes 챙기고 싶어요 (want), 챙길 수 있어요 (can), and 못 챙겨요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
챙기다.shortExplanation: 챙기다 means "to take care of" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 챙기다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 챙겨요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 들다 'to lift' for 'remember to bring an umbrella' — 우산을 들어요 means physically holding it up; 'grab/take it along' is 우산을 챙겨요.
Saying 밥을 먹어 to tell someone to take care of themselves, missing the nuance — Koreans say 밥 잘 챙겨 먹어 ('make sure you eat'), where 챙기다 carries the care.
Treating 챙기다 as only 'pack objects' and never using it for people; 아이를 챙기다 / 동생을 챙기다 ('look after') is just as common.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 챙기다 becomes 챙길 수 있어요 ("can") and 챙길 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not take care of.
I want to take care of.
I have to take care of.

usagePhrases.note: Grabbing the items you need before leaving

examples.en: Grab an umbrella!
examples.note: Bare casual reminder; object 우산 with no particle

examples.ko: 나갈 때 지갑이랑 열쇠를 꼭 챙기세요.
examples.romanization: nagal ttae jigabirang yeolsoereul kkok chaenggiseyo.
examples.en: Be sure to take your wallet and keys when you leave.
examples.note: 꼭 'without fail' + 챙기다 = don't forget to grab

examples.ko: 엄마가 매일 제 도시락을 챙겨 주시고 건강도 챙겨 주세요.
examples.romanization: eommaga maeil je dosirageul chaenggyeo jusigo geongangdo chaenggyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Mom packs my lunch every day and looks after my health too.
examples.note: Shows both senses: pack things AND care for a person

ex.en: I realized I had left my wallet behind.
ex.note: A realistic reason to return home.

지갑.nuance: 지갑(紙匣) is Sino-Korean — 紙 'paper' + 匣 'small box/case' — historically a 'paper case', now the small folding holder for your money, cards, and ID. Don't confuse it with 가방, which is the larger bag/handbag/backpack you carry items in: a 지갑 typically goes INSIDE a 가방. Modern usage has stretched 지갑 to digital things too — your phone's payment app is a 모바일 지갑 ('mobile wallet') — but the core image is the physical billfold. A subtle pitfall is the verb of forgetting: English 'I forgot my wallet' becomes Korean 지갑을 두고 왔어요 ('I put it down and came'), NOT 지갑을 잊어버렸어요 — 잊어버리다 is for forgetting information/facts (a name, an appointment), while physically leaving an object behind is 두고 오다. For losing it irretrievably you use 잃어버리다. Collocations: 지갑을 열다 (open the wallet → spend), 지갑이 가볍다/두둑하다 (thin/fat wallet = broke/flush), 지갑을 챙기다 (grab your wallet), 동전 지갑 (coin purse).
지갑.explanation: "wallet" is 지갑 (jigap). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 지갑이 있어요 ("I have a wallet"). Watch the particle attached to 지갑 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.
지갑.shortExplanation: 지갑 means "wallet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 지갑을 잊어버렸어요 for 'I forgot/left my wallet'. 잊어버리다 is for forgetting facts; for leaving a physical object behind, use 지갑을 두고 왔어요. To lose it for good, use 지갑을 잃어버렸어요.
Confusing 지갑 (wallet) with 가방 (bag). The small money holder is 지갑; the big carrier is 가방. 지갑 goes inside 가방, so they are not interchangeable.
Forgetting the particle when taking something out: it's 지갑에서 카드를 꺼내다 (out of the wallet), using 에서 for the source, not 지갑에 (which would mark a destination or static location).

usagePhrases.note: 있다 'have'; 이 because it ends in a consonant
두고 오다 'put down and came' — the set phrase for forgetting things

usagePhrases.en: I take a card out of the wallet

examples.en: My wallet is inside my bag.
examples.note: simple: 안에 'inside' locates 지갑 within 가방

examples.ko: 지갑을 집에 두고 와서 돈이 하나도 없어요.
examples.romanization: jigabeul jibe dugo waseo doni hanado eopseoyo.
examples.en: I left my wallet at home, so I have no money at all.
examples.note: everyday: 두고 오다 for forgetting + 하나도 없다 'not even one'

examples.ko: 지하철에서 누가 제 지갑을 훔쳐 갔어요.
examples.romanization: jihacheoreseo nuga je jigabeul humchyeo gasseoyo.
examples.en: Someone stole my wallet on the subway.
examples.note: real situation: 훔쳐 가다 'steal and take away', a phrase you'd need in an emergency

ex.en: After turning off the light, I closed the door.
ex.note: A natural leaving-home sequence.

끄다.nuance: 끄다 is the direct opposite of 켜다 and means to cut the power to a device or to extinguish a flame, so the same verb that turns off a lamp also 'puts out' a fire (불을 끄다 covers both). The conjugation is the key trap: 끄다 is a ㅡ-dropping (으 불규칙) verb, so when you add 아/어, the bare ㅡ vowel disappears and the ㅓ of the ending takes over — giving 꺼요 and past 껐어요, never 끄어요. English speakers also confuse 끄다 with 닫다 (to close): you 닫다 a door or app window, but you 끄다 the power; saying 컴퓨터를 닫다 wrongly means 'close the laptop lid', not 'shut it down'. Register is neutral — 불 꺼 to a friend, 불을 꺼 주시겠어요? to a superior. A subtler point: to merely silence a phone, Koreans say 무음으로 하다 or 진동으로 하다, not 끄다, because 끄다 means the screen goes fully dark. Natural collocations: 불·전등을 끄다, 핸드폰·컴퓨터를 끄다, 에어컨·히터를 끄다, 촛불을 끄다.
끄다.explanation: "to turn off" in Korean is 끄다 (kkeuda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 꺼요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 끄다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 불을 끄다 ("to turn off the light") — then reshape the same stem into 끄고 싶어요 (desire), 끌 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 꺼요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
끄다.shortExplanation: 끄다 means "to turn off" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 끄다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 꺼요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 끄어요 for the present tense — 끄다 drops its ㅡ before an ending, so it must contract to 꺼요 (past 껐어요).
Saying 컴퓨터를 닫다 to mean 'shut down the computer' — 닫다 closes a physical lid or window; powering off is 컴퓨터를 끄다.
Using 끄다 to mean 'put the phone on silent' — fully turning it off is 끄다, but silencing is 무음으로 하다 or 진동으로 하다.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 끄다 becomes 끌 수 있어요 ("can") and 끌 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem: ㅡ drop
conjugationTips.body: 끄다 loses its ㅡ vowel before 아/어, giving 꺼요 (the same drop turns 바쁘다 into 바빠요). The ㅡ never takes its own 어요, so don't add 어요 to the bare ㅡ.

usagePhrases.note: The set opposite of 불을 켜다; also literally 'to put out' a fire (불을 끄다 = extinguish flames).

examples.en: Please turn off the light.
examples.note: Simple polite request with softening 좀.

examples.en: I turn off the light before sleeping.
examples.note: Everyday routine; -고 links two actions in sequence.

examples.ko: 회의 중에는 휴대폰을 꺼 두시기 바랍니다.
examples.romanization: hoeui jungeneun hyudaeponeul kkeo dusigi baramnida.
examples.en: Please keep your phone turned off during the meeting.
examples.note: Formal real situation; 꺼 두다 = turn off and leave off.

ex.en: I changed the plan midway.
ex.note: A direct plan-change phrase.

중간에.nuance: 중간에 does not always mean the exact mathematical center. It often means midway or before the process was finished.
중간에.explanation: "in the middle; midway" is 중간에 (junggane). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 중간에 계획을 바꿨어요. ("I changed the plan midway."). Watch the particle attached to 중간에 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
중간에.shortExplanation: 중간에 means "in the middle; midway" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 중간에 for a completed first action. If the first action finished, use -고 나서.
For a location physically between two places, 중간 is a noun; this card focuses on timing.

usagePhrases.note: A direct match for a changed plan.

usagePhrases.en: I got a call midway while going.

examples.en: I took a short break in the middle of studying.
examples.note: The original action pauses before it is finished.

ex.en: I got a phone call.
ex.note: The incoming call can interrupt an action.

받다.nuance: 받다 is for receiving things, messages, help, service, or documents.
받다.explanation: "to receive" in Korean is 받다 (batda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 받아요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 받다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 문자를 받아요 ("receive a text.") — then reshape the same stem into 받고 싶어요 (desire), 받을 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 받아요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
받다.shortExplanation: 받다 means "to receive" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 받다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 받아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
받아 주세요 often means “please accept/take this,” not simply “please receive” in an abstract way.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 받다 becomes 받을 수 있어요 ("can") and 받을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

examples.en: I received a text.
examples.note: Past.

examples.en: Can I get a receipt?
examples.note: Shopping.

examples.en: I want to receive help.
examples.note: Need help.

ex.en: People are standing in line.
ex.note: 서 있다 describes a continuing posture or line state.

서다.nuance: 서다 means to stand or, for vehicles, to come to a stop. Because the stem already ends in 어, the 요-ending merges instead of doubling: you get 서요 and the past 섰어요, never 서어요 or 서었어요. Watch the two sister verbs: 서다 is the plain state/result 'to be standing / take a standing position', while 일어서다 ('rise to one's feet') stresses the motion of getting up from sitting — so 'please stand up (from your seat)' is 일어서 주세요, but 'please stand here' is 여기 서 주세요. For vehicles 서다 overlaps with 멈추다 ('to halt'); 멈추다 is more general and can describe machines or actions stopping, while 서다 is the everyday word for a bus or car pulling up. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: the location where you stand takes 에 (여기에 서다), not the object marker, and don't say 줄에 서다 — the idiom is 줄을 서다, treating the line as something you 'do'. Korean also has no separate verb for 'stand something up'; that meaning needs the causative 세우다.
서다.explanation: 서다 (seoda) = "to stand". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 서요 plus one useful sentence like 여기 서 주세요 ("Please stand here"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 서고 싶어요 for what you want, 설 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 서요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
서다.shortExplanation: 서다 means "to stand" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 서다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 서요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the doubled 서어요/서었어요 — since the stem ends in 어, it contracts with the ending, so the correct forms are 서요 and 섰어요.
Saying 줄에 서요 for 'stand in line' — the natural idiom treats the line as an object, so it must be 줄을 서요/줄을 섰어요.
Using 서다 to mean 'stand something upright' (e.g., 'I stood the bottle on the table') — 서다 is intransitive; for that you need the causative 세우다, as in 병을 세웠어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 서다 becomes 설 수 있어요 ("can") and 설 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: the spot where you stand takes 에 (여기에), often dropped in speech

examples.en: Please stand in front of the door.
examples.note: place + 에 marks where you take your standing position

examples.en: People formed a long line.
examples.note: 줄을 서다 is the set phrase for queuing; 섰어요 is the contracted past

examples.en: The taxi suddenly stopped in front of us.
examples.note: same verb = a vehicle coming to a halt

ex.en: The door is open.
ex.note: The open state remains.

열리다.nuance: 열다 needs an actor opening something. 열리다 lets the opened thing become the subject.
열리다.explanation: 열리다 (yeollida) = "to open; to be opened". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 문이 열려 있어요. ("The door is open.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 열리다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
열리다.shortExplanation: 열리다 means "to open; to be opened" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 문을 열려 있어요. The thing in the state takes 이/가: 문이 열려 있어요.
Use 열고 있어요 only when someone is actively opening it right now.

usagePhrases.note: The window became open and remains that way.

examples.en: The cafe door is still open.
examples.note: 아직 plus result-state is very natural.

켜지다.en: to turn on; to be on

ex.en: The light is on.
ex.note: The on-state remains.

켜지다.nuance: 켜다 is the action of turning something on. 켜지다 focuses on the thing becoming or being on.
켜지다.explanation: 켜지다 (kyeojida) means "to turn on; to be turned on". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 불이 켜져 있어요. ("The light is on."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 켜지다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
켜지다.shortExplanation: 켜지다 means "to turn on; to be turned on" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 불을 켜져 있어요. Say 불이 켜져 있어요.
Use 켜고 있어요 only when someone is in the act of turning it on.

examples.ko: 방에 불이 켜져 있어서 누가 있는 줄 알았어요.
examples.romanization: bange buri kyeojyeo isseoseo nuga inneun jul arasseoyo.
examples.en: The light was on in the room, so I thought someone was there.
examples.note: Result-state gives the visual clue.

ex.en: The door is in an open state.
ex.note: Names the state directly.

상태.nuance: 상태 (狀態, 狀 'shape/form' + 態 'condition') is the present condition of one specific thing — a person's health, an object, a system — captured at a moment. The sharp contrast is 상태 vs 상황: 상태 zooms in on the CONDITION of a single entity (건강 상태 'health condition'), while 상황 is the broader CIRCUMSTANCE/situation surrounding events (교통 상황 'traffic situation', 지금 상황이 복잡해요). Habitual partners: 상태가 좋다/나쁘다, 상태를 확인하다, 건강/배터리/도로 상태, ~한 상태 ('in a … state'). A handy grammar use: 술에 취한 상태로 = 'in a drunken state.' The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'the condition is good' is 상태가 좋다 ✓ (좋다 descriptive), never 상태를 좋다 ✗; and don't reach for 상황 when you mean one thing's condition.
상태.explanation: "state; condition" is 상태 (sangtae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 상태가 좋아요 ("the condition is good"). Watch the particle attached to 상태 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
상태.shortExplanation: 상태 means "state; condition" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 상태를 좋다 ✗ — 좋다 describes a state, so the particle is 가: 상태가 좋다 ✓
Using 상황 (broad situation) when you mean the condition of one specific thing → 상태
Forgetting the compound has no particle: it is 건강 상태, not 건강의 상태 in everyday speech

examples.en: The condition is good.
examples.note: simplest state sentence with 가

examples.ko: 요즘 잠을 못 자서 건강 상태가 안 좋아요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jameul mot jaseo geongang sangtaega an joayo.
examples.en: I haven't slept well lately, so my health condition isn't good.
examples.note: 건강 상태 + 안 좋다 (negated state)

examples.ko: 중고차라서 사기 전에 상태를 꼼꼼히 확인했어요.
examples.romanization: junggocharaseo sagi jeone sangtaereul kkomkkomhi hwaginhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Since it's a used car, I checked its condition carefully before buying.
examples.note: real-situation: 상태를 확인하다 about a physical object

ex.en: The road was jammed. So I was a little late.
ex.note: Use 그래서 after the cause has already been stated.

그래서.nuance: 그래서 links a cause to its natural result — 'so / that's why' — and is the first cause-effect connector a beginner must own. It is the sentence-starting cousin of the clause ending -아서/-어서 (피곤해서 일찍 자요 = 피곤해요. 그래서 일찍 자요). The sharp boundary to learn is 그래서 vs 그러니까: both can mean 'so', but 그래서 reports a plain consequence, while 그러니까 pushes a conclusion onto the listener and is what you use before a command or suggestion (피곤하지? 그러니까 일찍 자 = so go to bed). Two real pitfalls: first, 그래서 cannot head an imperative or a let's-form — 그래서 일찍 자세요 sounds off, so switch to 그러니까. Second, English 'so' can also mean 'very' ('so tired'); that meaning is 너무/정말, never 그래서. Keep 그래서 strictly for result.
그래서.explanation: 그래서 (geuraeseo) means "so; therefore". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 그래서 ("so / that's why"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 그래서 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
그래서.shortExplanation: 그래서 means "so; therefore" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 그래서 before a command: 비가 와요. 그래서 우산 가져가세요. Result-into-an-order needs 그러니까 — 비가 와요. 그러니까 우산 가져가세요.
Mixing it up with 그런데 (but / by the way). 그래서 = result; 그런데 = mild contrast or topic shift. They are not interchangeable.
Translating 'so tired' as 그래서 피곤해요. There 'so' means 'very', so it should be 너무 피곤해요; 그래서 only means 'therefore'.

usagePhrases.note: Points back to the previous sentence and names its result.

usagePhrases.en: I'm tired. So I sleep early.

usagePhrases.note: Casual nudge for the speaker to get to the point.

usagePhrases.en: So how did it turn out?
usagePhrases.note: Stock follow-up that asks for the outcome of a story.

examples.en: It's raining. So I'm taking an umbrella.
examples.note: Plain cause → everyday result.

examples.ko: 어제 늦게 잤어요. 그래서 오늘 너무 피곤해요.
examples.romanization: eoje neutge jasseoyo. geuraeseo oneul neomu pigonhaeyo.
examples.en: I went to bed late yesterday. So I'm exhausted today.
examples.note: Past reason leading to a present state — both verbs carry their own tense.

examples.ko: 길이 막혔어요. 그래서 회의에 늦었어요. 죄송합니다.
examples.romanization: giri makyeosseoyo. geuraeseo hoeuie neujeosseoyo. joesonghamnida.
examples.en: Traffic was jammed. So I was late to the meeting. I'm sorry.
examples.note: Real apology context — 그래서 supplies the excuse.

cluster.title: 그리고 vs 그래서 vs 그런데 vs 그러면
cluster.rule: Pick by the logical link back to the sentence you just said: 그리고 simply adds, 그래서 gives its result, 그런데 turns away from it, and 그러면 treats it as a premise ("if that's so, then…"). Note that in real speech 그런데/근데 is very often not contrast at all — it's just "by the way", a way to slide into a new topic.

example.en: I had dinner. And then I drank coffee.
It's raining. So I'm staying home.

members.when: soft contrast, or changing the topic

example.en: By the way, when are we meeting?

members.en: then, in that case, if so
members.when: reacting to what was just said

막히다.en: to be blocked; to be jammed

ex.en: The road was jammed, so I was late to the appointment.
ex.note: The subject is 길 or 차, not the late person.

막히다.nuance: 막히다 is the passive/intransitive partner of the transitive 막다 ('to block'): the -히- infix turns 'someone blocks X' into 'X gets blocked', so 막히다 is something that HAPPENS to a road, drain, or nose rather than something you do. For traffic this is the single most useful verb — 길이 막히다 / 차가 막히다 — and its opposite is 뚫리다 ('to open up/clear'), with 안 막히다 the everyday 'no traffic'. Do not confuse it with 막다 itself: 'I block the road' is 길을 막다, but 'the road is jammed' is 길이 막히다, and the particle flips from 을 to 이/가 accordingly. Register is plain and universal. Because the subject is a non-person, the polite/imperative-looking forms (막혀 주세요, 막힐까요?) are essentially never used about traffic. The big English-speaker trap is treating it as transitive: there is no 'I am blocked by traffic' with you as subject — Korean puts the ROAD in the subject slot (길이 막혀요), and you simply say 길이 막혀서 늦었어요 ('I was late because the road was jammed').
막히다.explanation: 막히다 (makhi-da) = "to be blocked". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 막혀요 plus one useful sentence like 길이 막히다 ("for the road to be congested"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 막히고 싶어요 for what you want, 막힐 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 막혀요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off.
막히다.shortExplanation: 막히다 means "to be blocked" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 막히다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 막혀요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 저는 막혀요 to mean 'I'm stuck in traffic'. 막히다 takes the ROAD as subject, not the person: 길이 막혀요, then 그래서 늦었어요.
Mixing up 막다 and 막히다. 길을 막다 = 'to block the road (actively)'; 길이 막히다 = 'the road is congested'. Watch the particle: 을 for the active verb, 이/가 for the passive one.
Using 막히다 for a person standing in your way. A person blocking you is 길을 막다 (they actively block) or 앞을 가로막다; 막히다 is reserved for roads, pipes, and noses.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 막히다 becomes 막힐 수 있어요 ("can") and 막힐 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: for the road to be congested
usagePhrases.note: 길 + 이 막히다 is THE everyday way to say 'traffic is bad'

examples.en: The road is congested.
examples.note: Core frame: 길 takes subject 이, the verb is intransitive

examples.en: The road was very jammed because it was rush hour.
examples.note: Everyday: 퇴근 시간이라 'because it's leaving-work time' gives the cause

examples.ko: 지금 출발하면 차가 막혀서 두 시간 걸릴 거예요.
examples.romanization: jigeum chulbalhamyeon chaga makyeoseo du sigan geollil geoyeyo.
examples.en: If you leave now traffic will be bad and it'll take two hours.
examples.note: Real situation: 막혀서 chains cause to the 걸리다 'take time' result

ex.ko: 버스가 고장 나는 바람에 오래 기다렸어요.
ex.en: The bus broke down, so I waited for a long time.
ex.note: A strong 바람에 cause because the problem was not planned.

고장 나다.nuance: 고장 나다 means a machine, device, vehicle, appliance, or system stops working properly. The broken item is the subject with 이/가: 휴대폰이 고장 났어요. 고장 내다 is the active/causative counterpart, meaning someone broke it. 망가지다 is broader and can describe physical damage, ruined objects, plans, or conditions; 고장 나다 specifically focuses on malfunction. Standard spacing is 고장 나다 because 고장 is a noun and 나다 is the verb.
고장 나다.explanation: 고장 나다 (gojang nada) means "to break down / malfunction." Use N이/가 고장 나다. If someone causes the damage, use N을/를 고장 내다.
고장 나다.shortExplanation: 고장 나다 is an intransitive malfunction (N이 고장 나다); 고장 내다 means someone broke it.
commonMistakes: Saying 휴대폰을 고장 났어요. The malfunctioning item is the subject: 휴대폰이 고장 났어요.
Writing 고장나다 as one word in careful writing. Standard spacing is 고장 나다.
Using 고장하다. Korean uses the noun + 나다 expression 고장 나다.
Confusing 고장 나다 and 고장 내다. 나다 happens to the device; 내다 means someone caused it.

conjugationTips.title: 나다 → 나요 / 났어요
conjugationTips.body: 고장 나다 follows 나다: 고장 나요, 고장 났어요, 고장 날 것 같아요. The active counterpart follows 내다: 고장 냈어요.

usagePhrases.note: Causative 고장 내다 when the speaker caused it.
A common next action after a breakdown.

examples.ko: 세탁기가 고장 나서 근처 빨래방에 갔어요.
examples.romanization: setakgiga gojang naseo geuncheo ppallaebange gasseoyo.
examples.en: The washing machine broke, so I went to a nearby laundromat.
examples.note: A practical household consequence.

examples.ko: 버스가 고장 나는 바람에 약속에 삼십 분 늦었어요.
examples.romanization: beoseuga gojang naneun barame yaksoge samsip bun neujeosseoyo.
examples.en: The bus broke down, so I was thirty minutes late for my appointment.
examples.note: -는 바람에 marks an unwanted cause.

examples.ko: 화면만 깨진 줄 알았는데 전원도 안 켜져서 완전히 고장 난 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: hwamyeonman kkaejin jul aranneunde jeonwondo an kyeojyeoseo wanjeonhi gojang nan geot gatayo.
examples.en: I thought only the screen was cracked, but it will not turn on, so it seems completely broken.
examples.note: Distinguishes visible damage from functional malfunction.

ex.en: We moved the gathering to next week.
ex.note: A natural result when everyone is late or the weather is bad.

모임.nuance: 모임 is native Korean, built from the verb 모이다 'to gather/come together' plus the noun-forming -ㅁ, so it literally means 'a gathering.' It is the broadest, most neutral word for people coming together for a shared purpose — a club, a reunion, a regular dinner crew — and unlike 파티 it carries no festive or Western flavor. The sharp contrast: 파티 is fun and event-like; 회식 is specifically a work-team meal; 모임 is the umbrella term that can be any of these in a low-key way, including serious or hobby groups (독서 모임 'book club', 동창 모임 'alumni reunion'). Particle logic mirrors other event nouns: 에 to attend (모임에 가요/나가요) and 이 to say one exists (모임이 있어요). The English-speaker pitfall is again 에서 with 가다 (모임에서 가요 ✗) — use 에 for the destination. A subtler point: because 모임 can name the standing group, 모임을 만들다 'form a group' is fine, whereas the same phrase sounds odd with one-off 파티.
모임.explanation: "gathering; meeting" is 모임 (moim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 모임에 나가다 ("to attend / show up to a gathering"). Watch the particle attached to 모임 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
모임.shortExplanation: 모임 means "gathering; meeting" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 모임에서 가요 to mean 'go to the gathering' — 에서 marks where an action happens; the destination needs 에, so 모임에 가요/나가요.
Forcing the English word 'party' onto every 모임 — a quiet hobby club or reunion is a 모임, not a 파티; choosing 파티 makes it sound like a festive event it isn't.
Using 하다 for joining (모임을 해요 to mean 'I attend') — to attend, use 모임에 나가다/가다; 모임을 하다 means the group itself meets/holds a session.

usagePhrases.en: to attend / show up to a gathering
usagePhrases.note: 나가다 'go out (to)' is the idiomatic verb for joining a regular group meeting

usagePhrases.en: to have a gathering (on the schedule)
usagePhrases.note: 이 marks 모임 as the thing that exists; 오늘 모임이 있어요
unlike 파티, 모임 CAN take 만들다 because you create the standing group itself
the qualifier (가족, 동창, 독서) tells you who gathers

examples.en: I have a gathering today.
examples.note: simple: 있다 + 이 to state that a get-together is on the schedule

examples.ko: 저는 한 달에 한 번 독서 모임에 나가요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun han dare han beon dokseo moime nagayo.
examples.en: I attend a book club once a month.
examples.note: everyday: 나가다 is the go-to verb for a recurring 모임; 독서 모임 = reading gathering

examples.en: I started a small group with my friends.
examples.note: real-situation: here 모임 is the standing club you create, so 만들다 'make' is correct

ex.en: The road was jammed because of an accident.
ex.note: A concrete noun cause for N 때문에.

사고.nuance: 사고 (事故, 'matter-incident') covers any sudden harmful event — car crashes, workplace mishaps, falls — and is the umbrella word a 교통사고 or 산업재해 sits under. The make-or-break contrast is purely grammatical and Koreans listen for it: 사고가 나다 (with 가) means the accident merely HAPPENED, assigning no blame, while 사고를 내다 (with 를) means the subject CAUSED it and is therefore liable — get the particle wrong and you may accidentally confess fault at the scene. Compare also 사건, which is an 'incident/case' in the investigative or criminal sense (a 살인 사건 is a murder CASE), whereas 사고 leans toward unintended mishap. Natural partners are 교통사고, 사고가 나다/내다, 사고 현장, and the everyday 접촉사고 (a minor fender-bender).
사고.explanation: 사고 (sago) = "accident". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 교통사고 ("traffic accident") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사고, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
사고.shortExplanation: 사고 means "accident" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't mix up 사고가 났어요 (an accident happened) with 사고를 냈어요 (I caused one) — the 를 version admits liability and your insurer will treat it differently.
사고 is the EVENT, not the people; the injured person is a 피해자 and the at-fault driver a 가해자 — never call a person a 사고.
Don't reach for 사건 when you mean an everyday crash; 사건 implies a criminal/investigative 'case', while a road bump is a 사고 (or 접촉사고).

usagePhrases.note: The single most common compound; written as one solid word, 交通事故.
나다 is the intransitive 'occur' — nobody is blamed, it just happened.
내다 (transitive 'bring about') marks the subject as the one at fault.
現場 'present-spot' = the exact place it happened; police seal it off.

examples.en: There's an accident up ahead.
examples.note: Bare frame: 사고가 나다, the neutral 'an accident occurred', nobody blamed yet.

examples.en: I caused an accident, so I called the insurance company.
examples.note: 사고를 내다 openly admits fault; the 가/를 swap is the whole meaning.

examples.en: If there's an accident, report it to 112 first.
examples.note: 112 is the police line; 119 is fire/ambulance — memorize both.

ex.en: I practice Korean in order to get a job.
ex.note: Noun plus 을 위해서.

취업.nuance: 취업 is the process or result of getting employment. 직업 is your occupation or job type, and 회사 is the company. For a purpose sentence, 취업을 위해서 or 취업하기 위해서 is natural.
취업.explanation: "employment; getting a job" is 취업 (chwieop). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 취업을 위해서 ("for employment / in order to get a job"). Watch the particle attached to 취업 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.
취업.shortExplanation: 취업 means "employment; getting a job" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 직업을 위해서 when you mean 'to get a job'. Use 취업을 위해서 or 취업하기 위해서.
Do not drop the object particle in the learner frame. Say 취업을 위해서, not 취업 위해서, until the full pattern feels natural.

usagePhrases.en: for employment / in order to get a job

usagePhrases.note: Common compound for preparing to get hired.

usagePhrases.en: to succeed in getting a job

examples.en: I practice Korean every day in order to get a job.
examples.note: Purpose plus daily practice.

examples.ko: 방학 동안 취업 준비를 할 거예요.
examples.romanization: banghak dongan chwieop junbireul hal geoyeyo.
examples.en: I will prepare for job hunting during vacation.
examples.note: Duration plus practical goal.

ex.en: I studied every day during the preparation period.
ex.note: 기간 names the period; 동안 marks what happens through it.

기간.nuance: 기간 is Sino-Korean 期間 (期 'a fixed term/appointed time' + 間 'interval') — a defined stretch of time with a clear START and END, such as an exam season, a vacation, a contract term, or a sale window. Contrast it sharply with 시간 時間: 시간 is generic 'time/hours/duration' you measure (세 시간 = three hours), while 기간 is a bounded named span you don't usually count in hours (시험 기간 = the exam period, not '×N hours'). Also distinguish 동안, which is the grammatical word for 'during/for' and attaches to spans (방학 동안), whereas 기간 is the noun naming the span itself (often combined: 방학 기간 동안). 기간 collocates with administrative life — 접수/신청 기간 (application period), 계약/임대 기간 (contract/lease term), 유효 기간 (validity period/expiry), 공사 기간 — and takes 에 ('within') or 동안 ('throughout'). The English-speaker pitfall: translating every 'time' as 시간 and saying ✗시험 시간이 길어요 to mean 'the exam season is long' — that actually reads as 'the exam's duration (one sitting) is long'; the season is 시험 기간.
기간.explanation: 기간 (gigan) = "period". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 시험 기간 ("exam period") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기간, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
기간.shortExplanation: 기간 means "period" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 시간 for a bounded span: ✗계약 시간 → ✓계약 기간, because a contract has a term (기간), not a clock-duration (시간).
Saying ✗기간이 걸려요 for 'it takes time' — taking time is 시간이 걸려요; 기간 names a fixed span and doesn't go with 걸리다.
Confusing 'how long is the period' (기간) with 'how much time' (시간): 유효 기간이 언제까지예요? (until when is it valid) vs 시간이 얼마나 걸려요? (how long does it take).

usagePhrases.note: 시험 기간이 길어요 = the exam period is long
방학 기간에 여행해요 = travel during the break
계약 기간은 일 년이에요 = the term is one year
할인 기간을 놓쳤어요 = I missed the sale window

examples.en: The application period ended.
examples.note: Official-notice tone; 접수 = receiving applications

examples.en: I learned a lot in a short period.
examples.note: 짧다 → 짧은; 기간 takes 에 to mean 'within that span'

examples.en: The road is blocked during the construction period.
examples.note: 기간 동안 = 'for the duration of'; everyday signage Korean

ex.ko: 한국에 머무는 동안 많이 연습할 거예요.
ex.en: While I stay in Korea, I will practice a lot.
ex.note: 머무는 동안 uses the verb modifier form.

머물다.nuance: 머물다 means to stay or remain somewhere for a stretch of time — a hotel, a friend's house, a city — and figuratively for a feeling or gaze that lingers (마음에 머물다). It is a ㄹ-stem (ㄹ-탈락) verb, the trap that trips up English speakers most: the ㄹ silently drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, giving 머뭅니다 and the polite request 머무세요, while the 어-form irregularly doubles to 머물러요 / 머물렀어요. The synonym boundary: 묵다 is the close cousin specifically for lodging overnight (호텔에서 묵다) and feels a touch more colloquial for 'put up at'; 있다 ('be/stay') is what casual travel talk actually uses — 호텔에 있어요 — while 머물다 sounds a bit more composed or written. Place takes 에, and a duration like 며칠 or 일주일 sits bare with no particle. The pitfall is regularizing the conjugation: not 머물습니다 and not 머물어요.
머물다.explanation: "to stay" in Korean is 머물다 (meomulda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 머물러요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 머물다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 호텔에 머물다 ("to stay at a hotel") — then reshape the same stem into 머물고 싶어요 (desire), 머물 수 있어요 (ability), and 머물 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
머물다.shortExplanation: 머물다 means "to stay" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 머물다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 머물러요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the formal form as 머물습니다 — the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다, so it is 머뭅니다.
Forgetting the 어-form doubles: it is 머물러요 / 머물렀어요, not 머물어요 / 머물었어요.
Putting a particle on the duration: say 며칠 머물러요, not 며칠을 머물러요 — the time span stands bare.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 머물다 becomes 머물 수 있어요 ("can") and 머물 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 머물다 has an irregular stem (ㄹ). Memorize its polite form 머물러요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the place of stay; the classic travel/lodging collocation.

examples.en: I'm staying in Seoul for a few days.
examples.note: Simple; 며칠 (a few days) sits with no particle.

examples.ko: 이번 출장 때는 친구 집에 머물렀어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon chuljang ttaeneun chingu jibe meomulleosseoyo.
examples.en: This business trip I stayed at a friend's place.
examples.note: Everyday; note the 어-form past 머물렀어요 (double 러).

examples.en: Tourists usually stay about a week.
examples.note: Real-situation, formal 합쇼체: the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다 → 머뭅니다.

ex.en: I will travel during vacation.
ex.note: A common period noun before 동안.

방학.nuance: 방학 is Sino-Korean 放學 — 放 'release/let go' + 學 'studies', literally 'releasing (from) studies', i.e. the official school break between terms (summer/winter). The crucial contrast is 방학 vs 휴가(休暇, 'leave/holiday'): 방학 belongs to the school calendar and applies to students/teachers, while 휴가 is the time off a worker takes from a job — a salaried adult on vacation is 휴가 중, never 방학 중. Also distinguish 방학 (a scheduled school break) from 휴일(休日, a single day off / public holiday like a national holiday) and 연휴(連休, a string of consecutive holidays). Note 방학을 하다 means '(the school) goes on break / break starts', an event, not 'I take a vacation'. The English-speaker pitfall is calling a working adult's trip 방학 (it must be 휴가), and forgetting that 'during vacation' uses the time particle 에 (방학에) or the duration noun 동안 (방학 동안), not 에서.
방학.explanation: 방학 (banghak) = "school vacation". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 방학에 ("during the break") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 방학, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.
방학.shortExplanation: 방학 means "school vacation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 방학 for a working adult's time off — that is 휴가. 방학 is only the student/school-calendar break.
Saying 방학에서 for 'during vacation' ✗. A time period takes 에 (방학에) or 동안 (방학 동안); 에서 is for places/actions.
Confusing 방학 (a multi-week term break) with 휴일 (a single day off) or 연휴 (a holiday stretch).

usagePhrases.note: Time point/period takes 에: 방학에 여행하다
School 'goes on vacation'; 하다 here = the break begins
Season + 방학; cf. 겨울 방학 'winter break'
끝나다 = come to an end; subject takes 이

examples.en: When is the break?
examples.note: Simple schedule question; 이에요 = 'it is'

examples.en: I want to go to Korea during the break.
examples.note: 에 marks the time; -고 싶다 = 'want to'

examples.en: I worked a part-time job during the break.
examples.note: 동안 = 'for the duration of'; a very common time collocation

ex.en: The purpose of coming to Korea is study.
ex.note: Names the idea behind 위해서 sentences.

목적.nuance: 목적 (目的, '目 eye + 的 target' — the target your eye is fixed on) is the conscious aim or intention behind an action, more deliberate and goal-directed than 이유 (the reason behind it) or 원인 (the cause that produced it). Compare the near-synonym 목표: 목표 is a concrete, often measurable target you aim to hit (this month's sales 목표, a finish-line 목표), while 목적 is the underlying purpose or 'what it is for' — a company's 목적 may be 'to help people' but its 목표 is 'sell 1000 units'. Register leans formal/written: it dominates immigration forms (방문 목적), reports, and mission statements. Two pitfalls: do not pair it with 하다 (you 이루다/달성하다 a 목적, you never 목적을 하다), and do not confuse 목적 (purpose) with 목적지 (目的地, 'purpose-place' — the destination, an actual place).
목적.explanation: 목적 (mokjeok) means "purpose, goal". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 여행 목적 ("purpose of travel"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 목적 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
목적.shortExplanation: 목적 means "purpose, goal" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 목적 (purpose, abstract) with 목적지 (destination, a physical place you travel to) — adding 지(地, 'place') changes the meaning entirely.
Use 이루다/달성하다 with 목적, not 하다: 목적을 이루다 ('achieve a purpose'), never 목적을 하다.
Don't use 목적 where 목표 fits: a numeric/concrete target ('my goal is to lose 5 kg') is 목표, while 목적 is the broader 'what it is for'.

usagePhrases.note: fixed phrase on immigration/visa forms; also 방문 목적 = purpose of visit
the right verb is 이루다 (accomplish) or 달성하다, never 하다
describes an intended aim behind an action; 뚜렷한 목적이 있다 = have a clear aim
Verb-는 것이 목적이다 states what the aim is

examples.en: What's the purpose of this gathering?
examples.note: Simple: asking for the aim of an event with 의 + 목적

examples.ko: 이 프로그램의 목적은 외국인을 돕는 것이에요.
examples.romanization: i peurogeuraemui mokjeogeun oegugineul domneun geosieyo.
examples.en: The purpose of this program is to help foreigners.
examples.note: Everyday: the N의 목적은 -는 것이다 framing that defines a purpose

examples.ko: 친구가 모임 목적이 뭐냐고 물어봐서 '그냥 같이 밥 먹는 거'라고 대답했어요.
examples.romanization: chinguga moim mokjeogi mwonyago mureobwaseo 'geunyang gachi bam meongneun geo'rago daedapaesseoyo.
examples.en: My friend asked what the purpose of the gathering was, so I answered 'just to eat together'.
examples.note: 방문 목적, 여행 목적 — '~ 목적' asks the aim/reason

ex.en: My Korean ability improved.
ex.note: 좋다 plus -아지다.

좋아지다.nuance: 좋아지다 is the adjective 좋다 (good) plus -아지다, the pattern that turns a state-word into 'become that state', so it literally means 'come to be good' — a gradual drift from worse to better, not a fixed quality. The key contrast is 좋다 vs 좋아지다: 좋다 just says something IS good right now (기분이 좋아요 = I feel good), while 좋아지다 reports a CHANGE toward good (기분이 좋아졌어요 = I feel better than before). It is warm and neutral in register, fine in both 반말 and 존댓말, and shows up constantly with 몸(body), 기분(mood), 날씨(weather), 사이(relationship), and 실력(skill). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 좋다 when you really mean a transition — 'My Korean got better' is 좋아졌어요, never 좋았어요, because 좋았어요 just means 'it was good (in the past)'. Note too that 좋아지다 means 'come to like' when the subject is a person feeling (그 사람이 좋아졌어요 = I came to like that person), so context decides between 'get better' and 'grow fond of'.
좋아지다.explanation: 좋아지다 (joajida) = "to get better". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 좋아져요 plus one useful sentence like 기분이 좋아졌어요 ("My mood got better"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 좋아지고 싶어요 for what you want, 좋아질 수 있어요 for what you can, 좋아질 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
좋아지다.shortExplanation: 좋아지다 means "to get better" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 좋아지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 좋아져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 기분이 좋았어요 to mean 'my mood improved' — 좋았어요 only means 'I felt good (back then)' with no sense of change; for the improvement you need 좋아졌어요.
Treating 좋아지다 like a normal adjective and trying 좋아지다예요 — it is a verb (좋다 + 아지다), so the present is 좋아져요, never *좋아지다예요.

Using 좋아지다 for someone improving a thing on purpose; 좋아지다 is intransitive (it happens by itself). To say 'I improved my grades' you act on them with a different verb — 좋아지다 only describes the grades themselves getting better.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 좋아지다 becomes 좋아질 수 있어요 ("can") and 좋아질 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Very common about feelings and health

examples.en: The weather got better
examples.note: Simple weather change, past tense

examples.en: My condition is getting better these days
examples.note: -고 있어요 shows the change is ongoing

examples.en: After taking medicine my body got a lot better
examples.note: -으니까 gives the cause of the improvement

ex.en: The meeting time changed to three.
ex.note: Useful for schedules and plans.

바뀌다.nuance: 바뀌다 is the intransitive twin of 바꾸다: the thing that changes is itself the subject (이/가) and nobody is named as the doer, so it covers things getting switched, replaced, or mixed up on their own. The dividing line vs 변하다 is key — 변하다 means a thing's inner nature transforms (사람이 변했다 = he's become a different person), while 바뀌다 means one item is swapped out for another (번호가 바뀌었다 = the number was replaced). Use 바꾸다 when YOU actively swap something (번호를 바꿨어요) and 바뀌다 when it simply ends up different (번호가 바뀌었어요). The 요-form is 바뀌어요 because the stem ends in the vowel 위, which won't contract — so spelling matters: it's 바뀌-, and the polite past is 바뀌었어요, never the wrong 바껴요/바꼈어요 that English speakers reach for by analogy.
바뀌다.explanation: "to change, to be switched" in Korean is 바뀌다 (bakkwida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 바뀌어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 바뀌다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 비밀번호가 바뀌었어요. ("The password changed.") — then reshape the same stem into 바뀌고 싶어요 (desire), 바뀔 수 있어요 (ability), and 바뀔 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
바뀌다.shortExplanation: 바뀌다 means "to change, to be switched" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 바뀌다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 바뀌어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 바뀌다 transitively — '번호를 바뀌었어요' is wrong because 바뀌다 has no object. If YOU did it, use 바꾸다: 번호를 바꿨어요.
Don't write the polite form as 바껴요 or the past as 바꼈어요; the 바뀌- stem keeps its 위 and gives 바뀌어요 / 바뀌었어요.
Don't blur 바뀌다 and 변하다: 마음이 바뀌었어요 = I changed my mind (switched decisions), but 마음이 변했어요 = my feelings have transformed (e.g., fallen out of love).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 바뀌다 becomes 바뀔 수 있어요 ("can") and 바뀔 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not change, to be switched.
I want to change, to be switched.
I can change, to be switched.
I have to change, to be switched.

usagePhrases.note: 바뀌다 = something gets switched/replaced by something else. The thing that changes takes 이/가, never 을/를.

examples.en: The meeting time got changed to 3 o'clock.
examples.note: Super common at work — schedules and times 'get changed' on you; note 3시로 with (으)로.

examples.en: Oh, the shop's name changed.
examples.note: ~네요 adds a 'huh, I just noticed' tone — natural the moment you spot a change.

examples.en: The plan might change again.
examples.note: 또 (again) + 바뀌다 is the everyday way to warn that things aren't fixed yet.

ex.ko: 회사 일 때문에 한국에 살게 됐어요.
ex.en: Because of work, I ended up living in Korea.
ex.note: A classic circumstantial 게 되다 sentence.

살다.nuance: 살다 means 'to live' in two senses — to reside somewhere and to be alive — and is a ㄹ-irregular verb. The stem ㄹ disappears before ㅂ, ㄴ, and the honorific 시, producing 삽니다 (not 살읍니다), 사세요 (not 살으세요), and 사니까; before vowel endings the ㄹ stays, so the polite present is 살아요. For where you live, the default particle is the static-location 에: 서울에 살아요. Interestingly, because living is an activity carried out over time, the dynamic-location 에서 is also acceptable and common, especially with hopes and experiences (한국에서 살고 싶어요) — this is one of the few cases where both 에 and 에서 work with the same verb. Contrast 살다 with 거주하다 (居住하다, Sino-Korean 'to reside'), a stiff, formal/written word used on official forms (거주지 'place of residence'); in speech you always say 살다. The English-speaker pitfall is keeping the ㄹ to say 살읍니다 instead of 삽니다, and reflexively choosing 에서 for every location when plain residence prefers 에.
살다.explanation: 살다 (salda) means "to live". Start from the polite form 살아요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 살다. A strong first sentence is 서울에 살아요 ("I live in Seoul"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 살다 also becomes 살고 싶어요 (want), 살 수 있어요 (can), and 못 살아요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then bend it.
살다.shortExplanation: 살다 means "to live" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 살다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 살아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Keeping the ㄹ before consonant endings and saying 살읍니다 / 살으세요 — as a ㄹ-irregular it drops: 삽니다 and 사세요.
Always using 에서 for the place you live — for stating a plain address, the static 에 is standard: 서울에 살아요 (에서 leans toward an active life-experience).
Using the formal 거주하다 in casual conversation — it sounds like a government form; everyday speech uses 살다.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 살다 becomes 살 수 있어요 ("can") and 살 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem: ㄹ
conjugationTips.body: 살다 is a ㄹ-stem word. The ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ endings: 살다 → 삽니다 (formal), 사는 (describing a noun), 사세요 (honorific). Before a vowel the ㄹ stays: 살아요.

usagePhrases.note: the place of residence takes 에 (static location), not 에서

examples.en: I live in Seoul now.
examples.note: residence with 에; 지금 'now' marks current address

examples.en: My parents live in Busan.
examples.note: honorific 사세요 for elders — note the ㄹ has dropped

examples.en: Someday I want to live on Jeju.
examples.note: future hope; 에서 + 살다 frames it as a life to be lived there

ex.en: Because of work, I suddenly ended up moving.
ex.note: A change caused by circumstances.

이사하다.nuance: 이사하다 specifically means relocating your residence — changing the home you live in — built from Sino-Korean 移徙 (移 'shift', 徙 'relocate') plus 하다. Contrast it sharply with 옮기다, which is just physically moving an object from one spot to another (책상을 옮기다 'move the desk'); you never use 옮기다 for changing homes, and you never use 이사하다 for shifting furniture. It splits into 이사 가다 (move away, focus on departure) and 이사 오다 (move in, focus on arrival near the speaker). Being a 하다-verb, the negative wraps the noun: 이사 안 해요 / 이사 못 해요, NOT 안 이사해요. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is treating it like English 'move' as a transitive verb — Koreans don't say '집을 이사해요'; the home is implied, so just 이사해요 is complete.
이사하다.explanation: 이사하다 (isahada) = "to move house". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 이사해요 plus one useful sentence like 이사 가다 ("to move away (to a new place)"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 이사하고 싶어요 for what you want, 이사할 수 있어요 for what you can, 이사 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests.
이사하다.shortExplanation: 이사하다 means "to move house" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 이사하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 이사해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 안 이사해요 — for 하다-compound verbs the negation goes inside, so the correct form is 이사 안 해요 (and 이사 못 해요 for inability).
Saying 집을 이사해요 by direct-translating 'move house' — 이사하다 already contains the idea of home, so the object is dropped; just say 이사해요.
Using 옮기다 for relocating yourself (e.g. 서울로 옮겼어요) — 옮기다 is only for moving objects; for changing residence use 서울로 이사했어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 이사하다 becomes 이사할 수 있어요 ("can") and 이사할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: to move away (to a new place)
usagePhrases.note: 이사 가다 stresses leaving toward a destination; pairs with 로/으로 for where you go

examples.en: I'm moving next month.
examples.note: Bare 이사해요 already implies changing homes; no extra object needed

examples.ko: 집이 좁아서 더 넓은 곳으로 이사하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: jibi jobaseo deo neolbeun goseuro isahago sipeoyo.
examples.en: The house is cramped, so I want to move somewhere bigger.
examples.note: Destination 'somewhere bigger' takes 으로, the direction particle

examples.ko: 이번 주말에 이사하는데 좀 도와줄 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: ibeon jumare isahaneunde jom dowajul su isseoyo?
examples.en: I'm moving this weekend, could you help out a bit?
examples.note: -는데 sets up the situation before the request — natural spoken framing

맡다.en: to take charge of; to be assigned

ex.en: I ended up taking charge of a new task.
ex.note: Good for work or school responsibilities.

맡다.nuance: 맡다 is the everyday native-Korean verb for taking on a role or responsibility — a task, a project, a part, even a saved seat. It feels more personal and active than the Sino-Korean 담당하다: where 담당하다 is the official 'assigned to me' on an org chart, 맡다 is the warm, often-volunteered 'I'll take this', so 제가 맡을게요 sounds team-friendly and proactive in a meeting. Crucial spelling and conjugation point: the stem ends in ㅌ, and it is a plain regular verb, NOT a ㄷ-irregular — so it stays 맡아요 / 맡았어요 / 맡을게요, and learners who mistakenly 'soften' the ㅌ to ㄹ (마라요, 마랐어요) are simply wrong. Its causative partner 맡기다 ('to entrust/hand over') flips the direction: you 맡다 a job yourself, but you 맡기다 it to someone else (저한테 맡기세요). Habitual collocations: 역할을 맡다, 책임을 맡다, 업무를 맡다, 자리를 맡다.
맡다.explanation: 맡다 (matda) means "to take charge of (be assigned)". Start from the polite form 맡아요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 맡다. A strong first sentence is 역할을 맡다 ("to take on a role"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 맡다 also becomes 맡고 싶어요 (want), 맡을 수 있어요 (can), and 맡을 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then bend it.
맡다.shortExplanation: 맡다 means "to take charge of (be assigned)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 맡다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 맡아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Not a ㄷ-irregular: the stem is 맡- (ㅌ), so it conjugates 맡아요 / 맡았어요, never 마라요 / 마랐어요. Don't soften the ㅌ.
Don't confuse 맡다 (you take the task on) with its causative 맡기다 (you hand the task to someone else): 제가 맡을게요 vs. 저한테 맡기세요 are opposite directions.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 맡다 becomes 맡을 수 있어요 ("can") and 맡을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not take charge of (be assigned).
I want to take charge of (be assigned).
I can take charge of (be assigned).
I have to take charge of (be assigned).

usagePhrases.note: 역할(役割) 'role'; 맡다 collocates with roles, parts, and duties you personally accept.

examples.en: I'll take that on.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ게요 = a willing commitment to the listener; sounds proactive and reliable.

examples.en: Assistant Manager Kim took charge of this event.
examples.note: Past 맡았어요 (stem ㅌ + 아) reports who got the assignment — note it is NOT 마랐어요.

examples.en: The department head entrusted me with that project.
examples.note: 맡기다 = causative 'hand over/entrust'; 저한테 marks the receiver — contrast with plain 맡다.
